title: Predictive Synthesis Framework for Elucidating Biophysical Cell State from Spatial Transcriptomics and Proteomics
title_norm: predictive synthesis framework for elucidating biophysical cell state from spatial transcriptomics and proteomics
abstract_text:
{
  "abstract": "The research domain of spatial omics focuses on the cross-modal synthesis of spatial transcriptomics and spatial proteomics at subcellular resolution to investigate cell state and fate. A critical scientific gap exists in understanding how the subcellular spatial organization of RNA and proteins independently predicts cell fate decisions, as current analyses treat these molecules as separate, abundance-centric measurements due to alignment difficulties and a lack of multimodal workflows. The primary objective is to develop a computational synthesis framework that builds a pipeline of image registration, grid harmonization, and multimodal embedding models to align paired spatial data into predictive biophysical fingerprints. Utilizing paired RNA and protein spatial maps from adjacent human cancer sections, the integration strategy corrects for non-rigid tissue distortion via diffeomorphic mapping to register molecular data into a common coordinate framework with shared pixel grids for one-to-one subcellular patch correspondence. This approach is significant because it shifts spatial omics analysis beyond abundance-only baselines by testing whether integrated RNA-protein spatial relationships provide early predictive signals for biophysical sub-states and lineage trajectories."

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence: molecular-level interactions among intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), multivalent domains, and RNA give rise to organelle-scale structures with distinct material properties (liquid, gel, solid) that dictate cellular function and disease. Despite an explosion of condensate-related data across structural biology, proteomics, imaging, and genetics, no unified framework connects sequence-encoded molecular grammar to emergent mesoscale material states and their functional/pathological consequences across the proteome. This proposal assembles a Working Group to synthesize eight distinct public data ecosystems—(1) condensate composition databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, CD-CODE), (2) IDR and phase-separation propensity predictors (PScore, catGRANULE, FuzDrop), (3) genome-scale interactome and co-complex data (BioGRID, STRING, hu.MAP), (4) subcellular localization atlases (Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell live-imaging library), (5) structural data from cryo-EM/ET of cellular condensates (EMDB), (6) single-molecule and FRAP-derived material-property measurements curated from literature, (7) disease mutation repositories (ClinVar, COSMIC) mapped onto condensate-forming proteins, and (8) evolutionary conservation data (UniProt, Pfam) across species. By integrating these previously siloed resources, we will build a computational framework—the Condensate Mesoscale Atlas (CoMA)—that links sequence features to predicted material properties, interactome connectivity, and functional/disease outcomes at proteome scale. Specific aims include: (1) constructing a harmonized, machine-readable dataset unifying sequence, structural, biophysical, and phenotypic condensate data for >2,000 human proteins; (2) applying interpretable machine learning and network-based approaches to identify sequence and interaction motifs (the 'molecular grammar') that predict emergent material states and multiphase organization (e.g., core-shell condensates); (3) testing whether disease-associated mutations preferentially disrupt predicted grammar features linked to material-state transitions (e.g., liquid-to-solid) implicated in neurodegeneration and cancer; and (4) validating framework predictions against independent public datasets not used in model training. This task exceeds single-lab capacity: it requires biophysicists who understand phase-separation thermodynamics, structural biologists interpreting cryo-EM data, computational biologists building predictive models, cell biologists validating localization/functional data, and clinicians/geneticists linking findings to disease—expertise no single laboratory possesses. NCEMS support is essential to provide computational infrastructure for harmonizing heterogeneous, differently formatted datasets, to convene the necessary interdisciplinary expertise, and to establish shared open-science standards for reproducible mesoscale data synthesis. All harmonized datasets, trained models, and analysis pipelines will be released as FAIR, versioned resources via GitHub and Zenodo, accompanied by interactive visualization tools for the broader community. The Working Group will recruit graduate students and postdocs from biophysics, computational biology, and cell biology backgrounds, providing hands-on training in multi-omic data integration, machine learning interpretability, and collaborative open-science workflows—directly cultivating the data-savvy, cross-disciplinary workforce NCEMS aims to develop. This synthesis effort promises to resolve a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biology: how simple sequence-encoded interactions give rise to complex, function-defining mesoscale organization, with direct implications for understanding proteinopathies and designing synthetic condensates.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation—exemplify mesoscale emergence: molecular-level sequence features and interactions give rise to micron-scale structures with material properties (viscosity, surface tension, exchange dynamics) that in turn shape cellular decision-making in stress response, signaling, and disease. Despite intense interest, the field lacks a unified, predictive framework linking intrinsically disordered region (IDR) sequence grammar to condensate composition, biophysical state, and downstream cellular outcomes. This gap persists not for lack of data—thousands of studies have generated condensate-component databases, high-content subcellular imaging atlases, proximity-labeling interactomes, cryo-electron tomograms, disease mutation catalogs, and AlphaFold-derived structural ensembles—but because these resources are scattered across incompatible formats, disciplines, and repositories, with no single lab possessing the expertise to harmonize and jointly analyze them. This working group proposes to close that gap through community-scale data synthesis.

We will integrate five previously siloed public data classes: (1) curated condensate-associated protein and sequence databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, PhaSePro); (2) subcellular localization and dynamics imaging (Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Allen Cell Explorer); (3) proximity-labeling and interactome datasets defining in vivo condensate composition; (4) biophysical/simulation resources describing IDR sequence patterning (charge, aromaticity, stickers-and-spacers architecture) including coarse-grained simulation parameter sets (e.g., CALVADOS-derived); and (5) disease-variant databases (ClinVar, COSMIC) mapping mutations onto IDRs linked to pathological condensate dysregulation. Using graph-based and deep generative models, we will construct a multi-layer network connecting molecular sequence features to condensate proteome composition, imaging-derived morphological/dynamic phenotypes, and organismal disease outcomes. A central analytical goal is to identify emergent “rules”—nonlinear, context-dependent combinations of sequence and interaction features—that predict when and where condensates form, what determines their material properties, and how perturbation (mutation, stress, drug treatment) shifts phenotypic outcomes across cell types.

This effort inherently requires cross-disciplinary integration beyond any single lab: polymer physicists and biophysicists to encode sequence-to-property relationships, cell biologists and imaging scientists to interpret phenotypic datasets, computational/AI scientists to build multi-modal integrative models, and clinical geneticists to connect molecular predictions to disease. NCEMS support is essential to convene this team, provide shared computational infrastructure for harmonizing heterogeneous ontologies (protein IDs, imaging metadata, mutation annotations), and establish reproducible, version-controlled pipelines. All harmonized datasets, trained models, and analysis code will be released as an open, queryable resource (a “Condensate Emergence Atlas”) under FAIR principles, enabling community reuse and extension.

Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across institutions, receiving hands-on training in multi-omic data integration, machine learning for biophysical prediction, and open/reproducible science practices, while rotating through partner labs to gain cross-disciplinary fluency. By synthesizing existing but fragmented public data at unprecedented scale, this project will resolve a long-standing puzzle in mesoscale biology—how molecular sequence information encodes emergent cellular organization—while producing a durable, reusable resource and training pipeline for the next generation of data-savvy molecular and cellular scientists.

Despite an explosion of public data describing condensate-forming proteins (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, PhaSePro), disorder and sequence features (MobiDB, DisProt), protein-protein and protein-RNA interactomes (BioGRID, STRING, RNAct), subcellular imaging (Human Protein Atlas, Cell Painting, OpenCell), and emerging cryo-electron tomography maps of native cellular architecture (EMPIAR, CZ Imaging Institute datasets), no unified framework exists to explain how molecular-scale features scale up to determine condensate material properties (viscosity, multiphasicity, exchange dynamics) and their downstream cellular consequences (transcriptional regulation, stress response, signaling compartmentalization). This gap persists because the requisite data are scattered across incompatible formats, curated by different scientific communities (biophysicists, structural biologists, cell biologists, and computational scientists), and require integration at a scale beyond any single laboratory's capacity.

This Working Group will assemble a transdisciplinary team—including soft-matter biophysicists, structural/cryo-EM specialists, cell biologists studying condensate function, and machine-learning/data scientists—to build an integrated, open-access Mesoscale Condensate Atlas that harmonizes sequence-level features, empirically measured biophysical parameters (partition coefficients, fluorescence recovery after photobleaching rates, viscosity estimates), interactome connectivity, and high-resolution imaging/tomography data across human, yeast, and model organism datasets. Using this atlas, we will address three synthesis-driven questions: (1) What combinations of sequence grammar (charge patterning, aromatic residue spacing, RNA-binding motifs) and interactome topology best predict condensate formation propensity and material state across proteomes? (2) Do condensates exhibit conserved scaling laws or percolation-like thresholds relating molecular valency/concentration to emergent material properties, and are these principles conserved across cell types and species? (3) Can integrated molecular-to-imaging data reveal generalizable ‘emergence signatures’—quantitative markers that predict when a condensate transitions from a passive assembly to one with regulatory or catalytic function at the cellular level?

We will develop novel network-based and generative AI models trained on this synthesized cross-scale dataset, producing publicly available, reproducible pipelines (via containerized workflows and FAIR-compliant repositories) that the community can extend to new proteins or organisms. This project requires NCEMS support because it demands sustained, coordinated data harmonization across incompatible legacy databases maintained by distinct research communities, computational infrastructure for large-scale multi-modal integration, and structured collaboration between biophysics and cell biology groups that rarely co-author work. The initiative will provide hands-on training for graduate students and postdocs in cross-disciplinary data science, biophysical modeling, and open-science practices, producing a new generation of scientists equipped to study emergence phenomena computationally. Ultimately, this work will establish generalizable principles governing how molecular-scale interactions generate mesoscale cellular architecture—a foundational advance for predictive cell biology.

Biomolecular condensates—membraneless organelles formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence, where local biomolecular interactions give rise to system-level properties (viscosity, surface tension, exchange dynamics) that dictate cellular function in transcription, stress response, and signaling. Despite an explosion of condensate-related datasets, no unified framework connects the molecular determinants of phase behavior (intrinsically disordered region composition, multivalent 'sticker-spacer' motifs, post-translational modifications) to emergent mesoscale material properties and their downstream cellular consequences. This gap persists because relevant data are scattered across incompatible resources: sequence/structure databases (UniProt, AlphaFold DB, MobiDB), condensate-specific repositories (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS, CD-CODE), interactome networks (BioGRID, STRING, IntAct), post-translational modification atlases (PhosphoSitePlus), protein abundance/localization maps (Human Protein Atlas, PaxDb), and heterogeneous imaging/biophysical measurements (FRAP recovery curves, single-molecule tracking, cryo-electron tomography from EMPIAR). No single laboratory possesses the combined expertise in biophysics, structural bioinformatics, network science, and machine learning required to harmonize these disparate data types into a predictive, mechanistic framework.

This Working Group will assemble condensate biophysicists, computational structural biologists, network scientists, cell biologists, and machine learning experts to build an integrated, open-access resource—the Condensate Emergence Atlas (CEA)—that links molecular-scale features to mesoscale phase behavior and cellular outcomes. We will: (1) curate and cross-reference sequence-based determinants (disorder content, charge patterning, aromatic sticker density) with experimentally reported condensate material properties (liquid, gel, solid; FRAP-derived mobile fractions; concentration-dependent phase boundaries); (2) integrate interactome and stoichiometry data to model condensates as emergent network phenomena, testing whether percolation-like thresholds in interaction valency predict phase transition points; (3) incorporate PTM and cellular context data (abundance, localization, cell-type specificity) to explain condition-dependent condensate emergence versus dissolution; and (4) apply supervised and unsupervised machine learning to identify generalizable 'rules' distinguishing functional condensates from aberrant aggregates linked to disease (e.g., neurodegeneration-associated solidification).

A central scientific question we will address: Can mesoscale material properties of condensates be predicted from molecular-scale sequence and interaction features alone, or do emergent properties require irreducible knowledge of cellular context (concentration, crowding, PTM state)? Answering this tests fundamental assumptions about reductionism versus emergence in molecular systems biology.

This project is infeasible for any single lab given the scale of cross-database harmonization, the breadth of required expertise, and the need for standardized ontologies bridging biophysics and cell biology communities. NCEMS support will fund coordinated data-wrangling sprints, shared computational infrastructure, and workshops to establish community standards for condensate data annotation. All curated datasets, harmonization pipelines, and predictive models will be released under FAIR principles via a public repository and interactive web tool. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across partner labs, receiving cross-training in wet-lab condensate biology, computational biophysics, and machine learning—directly cultivating the data-savvy, interdisciplinary workforce NCEMS aims to develop. Ultimately, this synthesis effort will yield a generalizable framework for predicting mesoscale emergent properties from molecular data, with broad applicability beyond condensates to other emergent cellular phenomena.

The team will integrate machine learning (graph neural networks trained on PPI topology plus sequence embeddings), coarse-grained biophysical simulation benchmarking, and image-derived phenotypic quantification to build predictive models that generalize across protein families and cell types—an analysis impossible without cross-disciplinary data fusion at this scale. Deliverables include: a unified, versioned 'Condensate Emergence Atlas' linking sequence, network, and phenotype data with open APIs; predictive models identifying condensate-prone proteins and mutation-driven emergent dysfunction relevant to neurodegeneration and cancer; and a reproducible open-source pipeline (Snakemake/Nextflow, containerized) for community reuse. The Working Group will comprise biophysicists, network scientists, cell biologists, and clinical genomics researchers from institutions varying in size and geography, explicitly recruiting early-career co-PIs and including graduate students/postdocs in every workflow layer, with structured training in reproducible multi-omic synthesis, FAIR data practices, and interdisciplinary communication. All code, harmonized datasets, and trained models will be deposited on public repositories (Zenodo, GitHub, Synapse) under NCEMS open science guidelines, enabling the broader community to test, extend, and apply this cross-scale framework to other emergent mesoscale phenomena beyond condensates.

Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation—exemplify mesoscale emergence: collective material properties (viscosity, surface tension, multiphase architecture, aging into gels or solids) arise from thousands of transient, multivalent interactions among intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), folded domains, RNA, and post-translational modifications (PTMs). No single lab possesses the expertise or bandwidth to harmonize these heterogeneous, differently-scaled datasets—spanning atomic structure to cellular phenotype—into a unified predictive framework.

This Working Group will assemble biophysicists, structural biologists, computational biologists, cell biologists, and data scientists to construct a curated, interoperable meta-database and companion machine-learning framework—CondensateAtlas—that integrates sequence features (IDR composition, charge patterning, PTM sites, RNA-binding motifs), structural/ultrastructural data (condensate size, shape, multiphase organization from imaging archives), interactome-derived compositional networks, and quantitative material-property measurements curated via natural-language-processing-assisted literature mining and manual expert curation. Statistical and generative modeling approaches (Gaussian process regression, graph neural networks trained on interaction networks, physics-informed biophysical polymer models) will be co-developed by computational and wet-lab collaborators to ensure biological interpretability.

This project requires NCEMS support because it depends on cross-institutional data harmonization, standardized ontology development for condensate properties, and computational infrastructure beyond any single lab's capacity, while uniting communities (structural biology, soft-matter physics, cell biology, genomics) that rarely interact directly. The working group will include early-career researchers and trainees who will lead specific data curation and modeling modules, receiving hands-on training in FAIR data practices, reproducible workflow design (Snakemake/Nextflow pipelines), and multidisciplinary team science. Biomolecular condensates—membrane-less assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence: they arise from collective, multivalent interactions among proteins and nucleic acids, yet exhibit properties (viscosity, selective permeability, catalytic enhancement, signaling thresholds) not predictable from any single component. Despite an explosion of condensate-related data across structural biology, proteomics, imaging, and genetics, no unified framework connects molecular-level sequence/structural features to emergent condensate behavior and downstream cellular phenotypes. This gap persists because the relevant data are fragmented across disconnected resources—intrinsically disordered region (IDR) predictors (MobiDB, IUPred), condensate component databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro, CD-CODE), structural repositories (PDB, AlphaFold DB), interactome networks (BioGRID, STRING, IntAct), subcellular imaging atlases (Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell), single-cell/spatial transcriptomics, and disease-variant catalogs (ClinVar, COSMIC). Synthesizing these heterogeneous, multiscale datasets requires expertise spanning biophysics, structural biology, cell biology, computational modeling, evolutionary biology, and clinical genetics—expertise no single lab possesses, and integration efforts that exceed what any two-lab collaboration could reasonably undertake.

This Working Group will construct an open, queryable 'Condensatome' resource and analytical framework that integrates these disparate datasets to answer a fundamental question: What generalizable molecular features—sequence composition, IDR architecture, multivalent interaction motifs, post-translational modification sites, and structural flexibility—predict the emergent mesoscale properties of biomolecular condensates (nucleation propensity, material state, compositional selectivity, functional output), and how do disease-associated mutations perturb these emergent properties to drive pathology?

Our approach proceeds in three synthesis phases. First, we will harmonize condensate component annotations, interaction networks, and structural/disorder predictions into a unified schema, applying network-based and machine-learning methods (graph neural networks, multivalency scoring) to identify molecular 'grammars' associated with distinct condensate material states and functions. Second, we will cross-reference these molecular grammars with imaging-derived phenotypic data (condensate size, number, dynamics from public live-cell datasets) and single-cell expression contexts to model how cellular environment (concentration, crowding, post-translational state) modulates emergent phase behavior across cell types. Third, we will overlay disease-variant data to test whether mutations disrupting predicted phase-separation grammar correlate with aberrant condensate formation implicated in neurodegeneration, cancer, and stress-granule pathologies, generating testable hypotheses for the broader community.

The Working Group will assemble investigators across career stages and institution types—biophysicists modeling phase behavior, structural biologists curating disorder/structure data, cell biologists with imaging expertise, computational scientists building integrative ML pipelines, and clinical geneticists connecting variants to disease—reflecting the transdisciplinary scope NCEMS uniquely enables. All harmonized datasets, trained models, and analysis workflows will be released as open, versioned, reproducible pipelines (via GitHub/Zenodo) accompanied by tutorials. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded as co-leads on data harmonization and modeling subprojects, receiving structured training in FAIR data practices, cross-disciplinary communication, and reproducible computational biology, directly building the data-savvy workforce this call seeks to cultivate while resolving a long-standing puzzle in mesoscale emergence.

This proposal assembles a Working Group of biophysicists, computational structural biologists, network scientists, cell biologists, and clinical genomicists to synthesize these disparate public resources into a unified, predictive, and mechanistic framework for condensate emergence. We will integrate: (1) sequence-derived features of intrinsic disorder, charge patterning, and multivalent motifs from UniProt, MobiDB, and IDRome conformational ensemble data; (2) curated condensate composition and phase-behavior annotations from PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro, LLPSDB, and CD-CODE; (3) protein-protein and protein-RNA interaction topology from BioGRID, STRING, and RNAct; (4) structural context from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database and PDB; (5) subcellular localization and condensate imaging data from the Human Protein Atlas and Allen Cell Explorer; (6) single-molecule and FRAP-derived exchange kinetics extracted from published literature and condensate databases; and (7) disease-associated variant data from ClinVar and COSMIC. Using this multi-modal resource, we will address three central questions: First, what combinations of sequence, network topology, and structural features best predict whether a protein participates in condensate formation, and do these features generalize across condensate types (stress granules, transcriptional condensates, nucleoli)? Second, does interactome topology (e.g., hub connectivity, clustering coefficients) correlate with emergent material properties such as liquid-to-solid transitions and exchange dynamics measured by FRAP? Third, can disease-associated mutations be systematically mapped onto this framework to identify variants that specifically perturb condensate emergence, and do such perturbations correlate with altered transcriptional noise or cellular phenotypes documented in single-cell RNA-seq datasets (ENCODE, Human Cell Atlas)? This synthesis requires computational infrastructure and cross-disciplinary expertise—spanning biophysical theory, network science, structural bioinformatics, and clinical genetics—that no single lab possesses, and it demands harmonization of heterogeneous, differently-curated public databases at a scale only achievable through coordinated collaboration. Deliverables include an open-access, version-controlled integrated database and machine-learning framework (CondensateAtlas), reproducible analysis pipelines, and a predictive model relating molecular grammar to emergent mesoscale phenotype. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across partner labs, receiving cross-training in biophysical modeling, network analysis, and open, reproducible data science, directly building the data-savvy interdisciplinary workforce NCEMS aims to cultivate.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—represent a paradigmatic mesoscale emergent phenomenon, arising from multivalent, low-affinity interactions among proteins and nucleic acids to produce compartments with distinct biophysical properties and cellular functions. Despite an explosion of data characterizing condensates across scales—from intrinsically disordered region (IDR) sequence features to interactome networks to live-cell imaging phenotypes—the field lacks an integrated framework connecting molecular grammar to cellular outcome. This proposal establishes a Working Group to synthesize disparate, publicly available datasets spanning five layers of biological organization: (1) sequence/structural databases of phase-separating proteins (PhaSepDB, PhaSePro, LLPSDB, CatGRANULE outputs); (2) proteome-wide interactome and post-translational modification data (BioGRID, PhosphoSitePlus, STRING); (3) cryo-electron tomography and super-resolution imaging datasets depicting condensate ultrastructure (EMDB, CZI Imaging Data Resource); (4) single-molecule and FRAP kinetic measurements of condensate dynamics deposited in supplementary datasets across hundreds of published studies; and (5) single-cell transcriptomic/proteomic data linking condensate-associated protein expression to cellular phenotypes and disease states (Human Protein Atlas, Human Cell Atlas, CCLE). No single laboratory possesses the computational infrastructure, biophysical expertise, and cell biology domain knowledge required to harmonize these heterogeneous, non-standardized datasets—many collected with different assay conditions, buffer compositions, and imaging modalities—into a unified predictive model. This is precisely the kind of large-scale, cross-disciplinary synthesis challenge NCEMS is positioned to catalyze. Our working group will bring together biophysicists specializing in polymer theory of LLPS, structural biologists with cryo-EM/ET expertise, computational biologists skilled in graph-based interactome analysis, and cell biologists studying condensate function in stress response, transcription, and neurodegeneration. We will develop a standardized ontology and data harmonization pipeline (leveraging FAIR principles) to align sequence features, biophysical parameters (saturation concentration, viscosity, surface tension), and phenotypic readouts into a unified multi-scale database. Using this integrated resource, we will apply machine learning and biophysical modeling to test three novel hypotheses: (i) whether condensate material properties (liquid vs. gel vs. solid) can be predicted from combinatorial sequence grammar and interactor stoichiometry; (ii) whether condensate emergence thresholds correlate with disease-associated mutations across cancer and neurodegeneration datasets; and (iii) whether evolutionary conservation patterns in IDRs predict condensate functional conservation across species. Deliverables include an open-access, versioned meta-database (deposited via Zenodo/GitHub with full analytical code), a generalizable predictive model of condensate emergence, and reproducible workflows adhering to community open-science standards. The project will directly train 4-6 graduate students and postdocs in cross-disciplinary data integration, biophysical modeling, and open science practices through structured hackathons and co-mentorship across participating labs. By synthesizing molecular-scale sequence data with cellular-scale phenotypic outcomes, this working group will resolve a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biology—how simple sequence and interaction rules generate the emergent complexity of condensate behavior—while establishing a template for future mesoscale synthesis research supported by NCEMS.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates—membraneless organelles formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—represent a paradigmatic case of mesoscale emergence, where collective behaviors of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs), RNA, and multivalent interactions generate organelle-like structures with functions not predictable from individual molecular components alone. Despite explosive growth in condensate biology, the field remains fragmented: sequence-based phase separation predictors, structural biology datasets, single-cell spatial atlases, and functional genomic screens exist in isolation, preventing a unified understanding of how molecular grammar dictates emergent mesoscale organization and downstream cellular phenotypes. This proposal assembles a transdisciplinary Working Group—spanning biophysics, structural biology, computational biology, cell biology, and machine learning—to integrate five classes of publicly available data: (1) curated LLPS driver/scaffold databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSepPro) and disorder annotations (DisProt, MobiDB); (2) structural and interaction data from the PDB, EMDB, and AlphaFold/ESMFold predicted structures, including cryo-ET tomograms of native condensates; (3) single-cell and spatial transcriptomic/proteomic atlases (Human Protein Atlas, HuBMAP, Tabula Sapiens) capturing condensate-associated protein expression across cell states; (4) high-throughput perturbation datasets (Perturb-seq, genome-wide CRISPR screens, ORFeome overexpression libraries) linking condensate-associated genes to cellular phenotypes; and (5) live-cell imaging repositories (e.g., OpenCell, LLPSDB) documenting condensate dynamics, material properties, and stress responses. No single dataset or lab possesses the breadth needed to bridge molecular sequence features to emergent mesoscale phase behavior and its physiological consequences—this synthesis requires simultaneous fluency in biophysical polymer theory, structural bioinformatics, single-cell genomics, and network-based phenotype mapping. Our central hypothesis is that a generalizable 'molecular grammar'—combinations of valency, disorder patterning, post-translational modification sites, and RNA-binding motifs—predicts not only condensate formation propensity but also material state transitions (liquid-to-gel-to-solid) that underlie both normal cellular function and disease-associated aggregation. We will develop multi-modal graph neural network models trained on integrated sequence-structure-interaction data, validated against independent perturbation and imaging datasets, to predict emergent condensate properties and their causal links to cellular outcomes such as stress granule dynamics, transcriptional condensate function, and neurodegeneration-associated aggregation. The working group will produce: (i) an open, harmonized multi-omic condensate database with standardized ontologies, (ii) predictive models and interactive tools for the community, and (iii) a mechanistic framework connecting molecular-scale grammar to mesoscale emergence and cellular phenotype. All code, harmonized datasets, and trained models will be released under FAIR and open-science principles via community repositories (Zenodo, GitHub, Biomolecular Condensates Knowledgebase). The project will train graduate students and postdocs in cross-disciplinary data integration, reproducible computational workflows, and collaborative team science, directly cultivating the data-savvy workforce NCEMS aims to develop while resolving a long-standing puzzle: how simple molecular rules give rise to complex, functionally consequential mesoscale organization in living cells.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence, where collective molecular interactions produce organelle-like structures with properties (viscosity, surface tension, selective permeability) not predictable from any single protein's biochemistry. Despite thousands of published studies characterizing individual condensates, the field lacks a unified, cross-scale understanding of which sequence features, structural motifs, and interaction network topologies causally determine condensate material properties and downstream cellular outcomes. This gap persists because relevant data are fragmented across incompatible resources: intrinsically disordered region (IDR) sequence databases (e.g., DisProt, MobiDB), condensate proteome catalogs (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, CD-CODE), protein-protein interaction networks (BioGRID, STRING), structural data from cryo-EM/cryo-ET and AlphaFold, quantitative live-cell imaging datasets (fluorescence recovery after photobleaching, condensate size/number distributions from the Cell Image Library and BioImage Archive), and single-cell transcriptomic/proteomic datasets capturing phenotypic consequences of condensate dysregulation in disease contexts (ALS, cancer). No single laboratory possesses the combined expertise in biophysics, structural biology, network science, computer vision, and systems biology needed to integrate these disparate data modalities into a predictive framework.

This Working Group will assemble a transdisciplinary team—computational biophysicists, structural biologists, imaging scientists, network biologists, and machine learning experts—to synthesize existing public datasets into an integrated, multi-scale atlas linking molecular grammar to emergent mesoscale behavior and cellular phenotype. Specific aims include: (1) Curate and harmonize condensate proteomic, sequence, and structural datasets into a standardized ontology capturing IDR composition, multivalency, post-translational modification sites, and predicted AlphaFold conformational ensembles; (2) Develop machine learning models trained on quantitative imaging-derived material property measurements (droplet fusion rates, FRAP recovery kinetics, aspect ratios) to identify sequence/network features predictive of condensate viscoelasticity and stability across previously siloed studies; (3) Integrate condensate composition data with protein interaction networks and single-cell omics to test whether network centrality and connectivity of condensate-resident proteins predict cellular sensitivity to condensate perturbation (e.g., in stress granule dynamics during disease); (4) Build a publicly accessible, version-controlled computational pipeline and interactive database (following FAIR principles) enabling the community to query molecular determinants of mesoscale emergence across cell types and organisms.

This synthesis requires NCEMS support because it demands reconciling incompatible data formats, resolving conflicting condensate classification schemes across independent labs, and computational infrastructure for cross-referencing structural, network, and imaging data at scale—tasks infeasible for any individual collaboration. The working group will recruit graduate students and postdocs from biophysics, computer science, and cell biology backgrounds, providing hands-on training in reproducible multi-omic data integration, FAIR data stewardship, and emergence-focused hypothesis generation. All harmonized datasets, trained models, and analysis code will be released as an open-source resource, establishing a reusable framework for mesoscale emergence research applicable beyond condensate biology to other multi-scale cellular phenomena.

Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence, arising from collective interactions among proteins and nucleic acids to produce organelle-like structures with distinct biochemical and mechanical properties. Despite an explosion of condensate-related data across genomics, proteomics, structural biology, and live-cell imaging, the field lacks a unified, quantitative framework linking molecular sequence features to network-level interactions and ultimately to cellular-scale phenotypes. Individual labs have generated fragmented insights—biophysicists characterize intrinsically disordered region (IDR) grammar in vitro, cell biologists document condensate dynamics via imaging, and systems biologists map protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks—but no systematic integration exists to explain why some proteins condense in some cellular contexts and not others, or how emergent condensate properties (e.g., material state, composition, responsiveness) scale with underlying molecular features and network topology.

This Working Group proposes to synthesize five previously siloed classes of public data: (1) sequence-based IDR and low-complexity domain predictions (e.g., from MobiDB, PONDR-derived datasets); (2) curated condensate/LLPS databases (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro) cataloguing experimentally validated phase-separating proteins and their in vitro conditions; (3) genome-scale PPI and co-expression networks (BioGRID, STRING, ProteomeHD); (4) quantitative single-cell imaging and localization atlases (OpenCell, Human Protein Atlas subcellular imaging, LLPSDB-linked microscopy) capturing condensate morphology, number, and dynamics; and (5) proteomic abundance and post-translational modification datasets (PhosphoSitePlus, PaxDb) that modulate condensation propensity in vivo. By harmonizing these disparate data types—spanning sequence, network, image, and abundance modalities—we will build predictive, mechanistic models of condensate emergence that no single dataset or disciplinary approach could achieve alone.

Our central hypothesis is that condensate emergence is governed by a combinatorial 'molecular grammar' operating simultaneously at three scales: intra-protein (IDR patterning, valency of interaction motifs), inter-protein (network connectivity, co-condensation partners), and cellular (local concentration, PTM state, compartment identity). We will use graph neural networks and multi-modal representation learning to integrate these layers, testing whether emergent condensate properties (size, number, material state, responsiveness to stress) can be predicted from lower-scale features, and identifying network motifs or sequence grammars that generalize across protein families and cell types. Validation will leverage held-out experimental datasets and cross-species comparisons (yeast, human, plant) to test universality of discovered rules.

This project requires collaboration among condensate biophysicists, network biologists, imaging data scientists, and machine learning experts—expertise no single lab possesses collectively—and NCEMS support for compute infrastructure, data harmonization workshops, and cross-database ontology alignment. The Working Group will include graduate students and postdocs in hands-on data integration, model-building, and reproducible workflow design, producing open-source pipelines, harmonized datasets, and a public condensate-emergence prediction resource. All code, integrated datasets, and models will be released under FAIR and open-science standards, providing a template for mesoscale emergence research broadly.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates are a central example of mesoscale emergence: weak, multivalent molecular interactions among proteins, RNAs, and metabolites can generate dynamic compartments with distinct material properties, compositions, and cellular functions. Yet a long-standing puzzle remains unresolved: why do some molecular assemblies form reversible, functional condensates, while others transition into aberrant, persistent, or disease-associated states? We propose a community-scale synthesis project to determine whether emergent condensate behaviors can be predicted from publicly available molecular features, interaction networks, cellular context, and perturbation phenotypes.

This working group will integrate existing public datasets spanning scales from sequence to cell state. Data sources will include curated condensate and phase-separation databases, intrinsically disordered region annotations, post-translational modification repositories, protein-RNA interaction maps, affinity and proximity interaction datasets, spatial proteomics, public live-cell imaging datasets, CRISPR perturbation screens, single-cell transcriptomic and proteomic atlases, and disease-variant resources. We will harmonize these datasets into an open, versioned knowledge graph linking condensate-associated biomolecules to physicochemical features, interaction topology, cell-type context, subcellular localization, perturbation outcomes, and reported material or dynamical properties.

The central scientific question is: what combinations of molecular features and cellular contexts give rise to distinct mesoscale condensate phenotypes, including nucleation propensity, compositional selectivity, fusion dynamics, stress responsiveness, and pathological persistence? To answer this, the project will develop interpretable machine-learning and network-based models that distinguish condensate classes and identify higher-order feature combinations not apparent from individual datasets. Particular emphasis will be placed on emergent properties that cannot be inferred from single molecules alone, such as multicomponent interaction density, RNA-dependent buffering, post-translational modification logic, and context-specific rewiring during stress, differentiation, or disease.

This effort requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory has the breadth of expertise or infrastructure to synthesize the relevant public data types at community scale. The working group will bring together cell biologists, biophysicists, RNA biologists, proteomics experts, imaging scientists, network theorists, machine-learning researchers, database curators, and trainees from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, and minority-serving institutions. NCEMS workshops will enable consensus building around condensate ontologies, metadata standards, uncertainty scoring, benchmark datasets, and reproducible analytical workflows.

Expected outcomes include: an open condensate emergence knowledge graph; benchmark datasets for predicting mesoscale condensate behaviors; interpretable models identifying molecular and contextual rules of condensate formation and maturation; and community guidelines for integrating heterogeneous condensate data. The project will train graduate students and postdoctoral fellows through team-based data synthesis sprints, reproducible workflow development, and cross-disciplinary short courses on open science, graph analytics, and AI-assisted biological discovery. All code, harmonized metadata, model outputs, tutorials, and manuscripts will be released publicly under open licenses.

By synthesizing diverse public data rather than generating new experiments, this project will address a fundamental question in molecular and cellular biosciences: how do molecular-scale features collectively produce emergent mesoscale organization that shapes cellular behavior? The resulting framework will advance predictive understanding of condensates and provide a reusable model for studying emergence across other subcellular systems.

(3) Which emergent condensate states are associated with beneficial stress adaptation, impaired proteostasis, altered signaling, or cell vulnerability? We will build an open condensate synthesis atlas that harmonizes heterogeneous public datasets into a FAIR knowledge graph connecting molecules, interactions, modifications, imaging phenotypes, perturbations, and cellular outcomes. Analytical innovations will include multimodal representation learning for combining images and omics, graph-based causal discovery to separate correlates from candidate drivers, biophysically informed machine learning features such as disorder, multivalency, charge patterning, and interaction valence, and community benchmark tasks for predicting condensate localization and phenotype transitions. Biomolecular condensates are paradigmatic mesoscale structures: they emerge from weak, multivalent molecular interactions yet can reorganize signaling, transcription, RNA metabolism, stress responses, and disease phenotypes. Despite thousands of studies, the field lacks a predictive synthesis explaining why the same protein can form a condensate in one cellular context but remain diffuse in another, or when condensate formation produces measurable cellular outcomes. This working group will integrate publicly available molecular, imaging, and functional genomic data to answer a central question: What combinations of molecular grammar, cellular state, and interaction context are sufficient to predict the emergence and phenotypic consequences of biomolecular condensates?

We will build an open, cross-scale Condensate Emergence Atlas by harmonizing existing datasets that are currently siloed across disciplines. Molecular features will be extracted from public protein sequence resources, AlphaFold structures, intrinsically disordered region annotations, post-translational modification databases, RNA-binding datasets, protein-protein interaction maps, and condensate-specific repositories such as PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS, and curated literature-derived annotations. Mesoscale localization and morphology will be synthesized from public imaging resources including the Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Allen Cell Explorer, BioImage Archive, and published high-content microscopy datasets. Cellular state and outcome layers will incorporate public transcriptomics, proteomics, stress-response time courses, Perturb-seq and CRISPR screen datasets, DepMap dependencies, and disease-associated variant resources.

The project will develop reusable analytical strategies for emergence research. First, we will create controlled vocabularies and probabilistic labels for condensate presence, morphology, dynamics, and cellular context, explicitly representing uncertainty across datasets. Second, we will use interpretable machine learning and graph-based models to connect molecular features, interaction networks, RNA context, post-translational modifications, and cell-state variables to observed mesoscale condensate formation. Third, we will test whether inferred condensate states explain higher-level cellular outcomes, such as stress survival, transcriptional rewiring, growth defects, and disease variant impact, beyond predictions from single-molecule properties alone. The central deliverable will be a set of open models that distinguish generalizable principles from dataset-specific artifacts and generate prioritized, experimentally testable hypotheses for the broader community.

This synthesis requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory has the combined expertise or infrastructure to integrate image analysis, protein biophysics, RNA biology, cell biology, network science, functional genomics, and open-science software engineering at this scale. The working group will include condensate biologists, computational biophysicists, bioimage analysts, data curators, machine-learning researchers, cell-state and genomics experts, and trainees from research-intensive and primarily undergraduate institutions. NCEMS working sessions will be used to establish shared data standards, perform collaborative model benchmarking, train graduate students and postdocs in reproducible synthesis workflows, and engage community stakeholders who maintain relevant public resources.

All products will follow open science principles: curated metadata, harmonized feature tables, analysis notebooks, containerized workflows, model code, benchmark datasets, and interactive visualizations will be released publicly with clear documentation and community contribution mechanisms.   "Within the domain of molecular and cellular biology, biomolecular condensates are studied to understand their emergence, material states, dynamics, and phenotypic consequences. However, the specific contexts that determine when condensates form, their adopted material states, and whether they buffer, transmit, or amplify cellular stress remain unresolved due to fragmented data that obscures necessary determinants like stoichiometry and network connectivity. To determine the combinations of molecular grammar, cellular context, and interaction-network architecture that drive condensate emergence, this study utilizes a secondary data synthesis approach employing foundation-model embeddings and graph neural networks. By modeling condensates as context-dependent emergent systems rather than static component lists, this research will elucidate why structurally similar proteins exhibit different behaviors and how protective condensates transition into pathological aggregates."

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates exemplify mesoscale emergence: weak molecular interactions among proteins, RNAs, metabolites, and membranes produce dynamic compartments whose collective properties cannot be inferred from any single component. Despite thousands of public datasets on protein localization, phase separation, RNA binding, perturbation phenotypes, and disease variation, a central question remains unresolved: what molecular and cellular contexts determine when condensates form, what material states they adopt, and whether they buffer, transmit, or amplify cellular stress? This working group will synthesize publicly available data to build and test an integrative, predictive framework for condensate emergence across human cells and model organisms.

The project will assemble a community-scale team spanning molecular biophysics, cell biology, RNA biology, proteomics, microscopy, machine learning, network science, and open-science infrastructure. The group will integrate existing public resources including LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, DisProt, AlphaFold and protein language model embeddings, ENCODE and RNA-binding protein datasets, Human Protein Atlas and OpenCell subcellular localization images, BioImage Archive microscopy datasets, PRIDE and ProteomeXchange proteomics, public stress-response transcriptomics, CRISPR perturbation screens from DepMap and BioGRID ORCS, and ClinVar/gnomAD disease variant annotations. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, the working group will harmonize these heterogeneous datasets into a FAIR, versioned condensate-emergence knowledge graph linking molecular features, interaction networks, cellular state, mesoscale morphology, dynamics, and phenotypic outcomes.

The core scientific innovation is to treat condensates not merely as lists of phase-separating proteins, but as emergent systems whose properties depend on multivalent molecular grammar, expression stoichiometry, post-translational modification potential, RNA context, interaction network topology, and cellular stress history. We will develop transparent AI and statistical models to predict three linked outcomes: condensate membership, emergent material or morphological class, and downstream cellular consequence after perturbation. By comparing predictions across stress granules, nucleoli, transcriptional condensates, P bodies, nuclear speckles, and disease-associated aggregates, we will test whether shared rules govern distinct condensate systems or whether each represents a context-specific emergent regime. A special focus will be placed on long-standing puzzles, including why proteins with similar intrinsically disordered regions produce different condensate behaviors, why some condensates are protective while others become pathological, and how disease mutations shift mesoscale organization without necessarily altering canonical molecular function.

NCEMS support is essential because the project requires coordinated synthesis beyond the scope of any single laboratory: cross-dataset ontology alignment, image-derived feature extraction, multimodal model development, biological interpretation across condensate classes, and community governance for reusable data products. Working-group meetings will produce shared standards for condensate metadata, benchmark datasets, reproducible workflows, and open tutorials. Trainees from diverse institutions will be embedded in cross-disciplinary subteams and trained in data integration, responsible AI, reproducible workflow design, and collaborative synthesis science.

All outputs will be released openly, including curated datasets, code, model cards, workflow containers, documentation, and interactive visualization tools. The expected outcome is a generalizable synthesis framework for predicting how molecular-scale properties give rise to mesoscale condensate behavior and cellular phenotypes, providing a foundational resource for emergence-focused molecular and cellular biology.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates are mesoscale assemblies that emerge from multivalent molecular interactions, yet their organizing principles remain difficult to generalize across cell types, stresses, and organisms. A central unresolved question is: which combinations of molecular features, cellular context, and environmental perturbations cause condensates to transition from adaptive, dynamic assemblies to dysfunctional states that alter gene expression, signaling, or viability? This working group will synthesize publicly available data to build a predictive, open atlas linking condensate composition, material properties, spatial organization, and cellular outcomes. The project will integrate existing datasets from proteomics of stress granules, nucleoli, P-bodies, transcriptional condensates, and disease-associated aggregates; fluorescence imaging and image-derived phenotypes from resources such as the Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Cell Painting, and Image Data Resource; public perturbation data including CRISPR screens, Perturb-seq, LINCS, DepMap, and stress-response transcriptomics; and curated databases of intrinsically disordered regions, post-translational modifications, RNA-binding proteins, phase-separation assays, protein interaction networks, and disease variants. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, the group will harmonize heterogeneous datasets into a common representation of condensate-associated mesoscale states. We will develop graph- and representation-learning approaches that combine molecular features, interaction topology, localization patterns, perturbation responses, and phenotypic readouts to identify recurrent ‘condensate state modules.’ These modules will be tested computationally for conservation across organisms, sensitivity to stress, enrichment for disease variants, and association with emergent cellular phenotypes such as translational repression, transcriptional bursting, DNA damage response, senescence, or toxicity. A key innovation is to move beyond cataloging condensate components toward identifying emergent state rules: for example, whether specific combinations of low-complexity sequence composition, RNA abundance, phosphorylation potential, network centrality, and local concentration predict reversible assembly versus persistent pathological aggregation. The project requires NCEMS support because it exceeds the capacity of a single laboratory: it demands coordinated expertise in cell biology, biophysics, proteomics, microscopy, RNA biology, network science, machine learning, ontology development, and open-science infrastructure. The working group will include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, national data resources, and computational biology groups, with structured roles for graduate students and postdoctoral fellows. Trainees will receive hands-on training in FAIR data curation, reproducible workflow design, cloud-based analysis, image feature extraction, and interpretable AI. Deliverables will include an openly accessible condensate-state knowledge graph, reusable analysis pipelines, benchmark datasets for predicting condensate behavior, community-developed metadata standards for condensate-related public data, and a synthesis manuscript defining cross-system principles of condensate emergence. By transforming dispersed public datasets into a unified framework, this project will address a fundamental mystery in molecular and cellular biosciences: how collective mesoscale assemblies acquire properties not predictable from individual molecules alone, and how those emergent properties propagate upward to shape cellular physiology and disease.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates are a defining mesoscale phenomenon: dynamic assemblies arise from many weak molecular interactions, yet display emergent properties such as selective partitioning, viscoelasticity, spatial organization, and regulatory influence on transcription, RNA metabolism, stress responses, and signaling. Despite rapid progress, a central unresolved question remains: which molecular features and cellular contexts determine when condensates form adaptive regulatory hubs versus pathological or dysfunctional assemblies? This working group will synthesize publicly available molecular, imaging, and perturbational data to build an open, cross-scale atlas linking condensate composition and physicochemical features to cellular outcomes across organisms, cell types, stresses, and disease states.

The project will integrate existing datasets from public repositories including the Human Protein Atlas, BioImage Archive, Cell Painting and fluorescence microscopy datasets, PRIDE and MassIVE proteomics studies, ENCODE and GEO transcriptomic and chromatin datasets, DepMap and CRISPR perturbation screens, LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, DisProt, AlphaFold structural models, and published condensate interactomes. We will harmonize heterogeneous data describing protein localization, intrinsic disorder, multivalency, post-translational modification, RNA-binding capacity, expression stoichiometry, interaction networks, and perturbation phenotypes. Using graph-based data integration, weakly supervised computer vision, representation learning, and interpretable machine learning, we will identify combinations of molecular features and environmental conditions that predict emergent condensate behaviors such as stress-induced assembly, nucleolar or nuclear body reorganization, granule persistence, and links to phenotypes including growth, differentiation, viral response, neurodegeneration, and cancer vulnerability.

The core scientific goal is to move beyond single-condensate case studies toward general principles of mesoscale emergence. We will test three synthesis questions: (1) Are there conserved molecular “design rules” that distinguish reversible functional condensates from persistent disease-associated assemblies? (2) How do changes in expression, modification state, and interaction-network topology combine nonlinearly to produce condensate formation or dissolution? (3) Can condensate-level properties explain cellular phenotypes that are not predictable from individual protein abundance or interaction data alone? The resulting models will generate community-testable hypotheses, such as specific combinations of low-complexity domains, RNA availability, phosphorylation sites, and network position that confer context-dependent condensate behavior.

This project requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory can curate, standardize, and analyze the breadth of imaging, proteomic, structural, genomic, and perturbation data needed to infer general principles of condensate emergence. The working group will assemble cell biologists, biophysicists, RNA biologists, proteomics experts, imaging scientists, data curators, machine-learning researchers, statisticians, and trainees from research-intensive, primarily undergraduate, and minority-serving institutions. NCEMS working group meetings will enable consensus development on metadata standards, benchmark tasks, uncertainty reporting, and interpretable modeling strategies.

All products will follow open science principles: harmonized datasets, code, model weights, workflows, documentation, and interactive visualizations will be released through public repositories with reproducible containers and community governance. Trainees will participate in cross-disciplinary analysis sprints, receive training in FAIR data stewardship, image analysis, network science, and responsible AI, and co-lead open tutorials for the broader community. By synthesizing existing public data at community scale, this project will provide a predictive framework for how molecular features give rise to emergent mesoscale condensate states and how those states shape cellular function.

Rather than generating new experimental data, the project will harmonize and reanalyze these resources to ask: which combinations of molecular grammar, interaction network topology, expression context, and environmental perturbation are sufficient to predict condensate assembly, dissolution, localization, material maturation, and cellular consequences?

The analytical strategy will combine expertise from molecular biophysics, cell biology, RNA biology, image analysis, machine learning, network science, and open-source software engineering. We will first create an interoperable condensate knowledge graph connecting molecular components, sequence features, interaction evidence, perturbations, imaging-derived phenotypes, and cellular outcomes using transparent provenance standards. Second, we will develop reusable computer vision workflows to extract mesoscale condensate phenotypes from public microscopy data, including size distributions, number, spatial organization, coalescence signatures, and temporal reversibility where time-lapse data exist. Third, we will train interpretable multimodal AI models to identify predictive rules for condensate emergence and state transitions, explicitly testing whether conserved mesoscale behaviors can be inferred from molecular features across different biological contexts. Finally, we will perform cross-dataset validation using held-out perturbation and disease datasets to identify general principles and context-specific exceptions.

We will release curated datasets, ontologies, analysis notebooks, trained models, image-analysis pipelines, and benchmark tasks through public repositories with documented metadata and community governance. The project will also produce training modules on multimodal biological data synthesis, interpretable AI, and reproducible mesoscale cell biology. By transforming fragmented public datasets into a coherent predictive resource, this project will provide mechanistic insight into how molecular properties generate emergent condensate states and how those states influence cellular adaptation, dysfunction, and disease.

title: Predicting Emergent Mesoscale Biomolecular Condensates from Public Proteomic, Imaging, and Perturbation Data
title_norm: predicting emergent mesoscale biomolecular condensates from public proteomic imaging and perturbation data
abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates such as stress granules, nucleoli, P-bodies, transcriptional hubs, and DNA repair foci exemplify emergence in cell biology: collective mesoscale assemblies arise from multivalent molecular interactions and generate new spatial, kinetic, and regulatory properties not predictable from individual components alone. Despite intense study, the field lacks a general, data-driven framework for predicting when specific proteins and RNAs will form condensates, how condensate material properties vary across cellular contexts, and which emergent assemblies causally influence cell state. This Working Group will synthesize publicly available datasets to answer a central question: what combinations of molecular features, interaction network architecture, expression stoichiometry, and cellular context predict the emergence and functional consequences of mesoscale condensates in human cells?

The project will integrate existing public resources that are individually powerful but rarely analyzed together: subcellular localization images from the Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Image Data Resource, and Cell Painting datasets; protein-protein and protein-RNA interaction maps from BioGRID, IntAct, STRING, ENCODE, POSTAR, and published AP-MS, BioID, and CLIP-seq studies; sequence-derived features including intrinsically disordered regions, low-complexity domains, charge patterning, prion-like domains, and multivalent motifs; transcriptomic and proteomic abundance data from GTEx, DepMap, PRIDE, ProteomeXchange, and single-cell atlases; and public perturbation datasets including CRISPR screens, Perturb-seq, stress-response time courses, and drug response studies. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, the group will create harmonized, FAIR data products linking molecular composition, imaging-derived mesoscale phenotypes, interaction networks, and cellular outcomes.

Our analytical strategy will combine computer vision, network science, statistical physics-inspired descriptors, and interpretable machine learning. First, we will use reproducible image-analysis pipelines to extract condensate-related phenotypes from public microscopy data, including puncta number, size distributions, co-localization, spatial organization, and context-dependent relocalization. Second, we will build multilayer interaction and feature networks capturing sequence grammar, binding multiplicity, RNA association, abundance, and compartmental localization. Third, we will train and benchmark models that predict condensate membership, condition-specific assembly, and emergent mesoscale phenotypes from molecular and network features. Finally, we will connect predicted condensate states to cellular outcomes such as stress survival, transcriptional reprogramming, proliferation, and disease-associated vulnerability using public perturbational and phenotypic datasets.

This synthesis requires NCEMS support because it is beyond the scope of a single laboratory: it demands coordinated expertise in condensate biology, cell imaging, RNA biology, proteomics, biophysics, machine learning, network theory, and open-science software engineering. The Working Group will include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and national data repositories, with active roles for graduate students and postdoctoral fellows. Trainees will receive hands-on training in reproducible workflows, metadata harmonization, image analysis, machine learning, and collaborative team science.

Expected outputs include an open atlas of predicted and observed human condensate-forming systems, validated computational workflows, benchmark datasets for community model development, and testable hypotheses about how molecular-scale properties give rise to mesoscale organization and higher-order cell behavior. By transforming fragmented public data into an integrated predictive framework, this project will address a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biology: how dynamic molecular interactions generate emergent cellular organization.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates exemplify emergence in molecular and cellular biology: weak, multivalent molecular interactions produce mesoscale assemblies with properties not predictable from individual components alone, including selective partitioning, altered reaction kinetics, and coordinated cellular responses. Despite rapid growth in condensate research, the field lacks a general, data-driven framework for predicting when a protein or RNA will participate in condensates, what mesoscale state will emerge, and how that state influences cellular phenotypes. This working group will synthesize publicly available datasets to answer a central question: which molecular features and cellular contexts jointly determine emergent condensate behavior and downstream cell-state outcomes? We will integrate complementary public resources spanning molecular sequence, structure, localization, interaction, and phenotype. Data sources will include condensate and phase-separation databases, AlphaFold and Protein Data Bank structural models, UniProt and RNAcentral annotations, BioGRID and STRING interaction networks, OpenCell and Human Protein Atlas subcellular localization images, BioImage Archive datasets of stress granules and nuclear bodies, PRIDE proteomics, ENCODE and GEO transcriptomic data, LINCS perturbational signatures, and genome-scale CRISPR or RNAi screens from DepMap and related repositories. The project will not generate new experimental data; instead, it will harmonize heterogeneous public datasets into an open, versioned condensate-emergence knowledge graph linking molecular features to mesoscale assemblies and phenotypic consequences. The working group will develop transparent analytical strategies combining computer vision, protein language models, graph machine learning, causal inference, and physical feature engineering. Image-based models will quantify condensate morphology, number, size distributions, coarsening, and spatial relationships across published microscopy datasets. Sequence and structure models will extract multivalency, disorder, charge patterning, interaction motifs, RNA-binding potential, and post-translational modification sites. Network and perturbation analyses will test whether emergent condensate states mediate cellular outcomes such as stress resistance, transcriptional repression, cell-cycle arrest, viral infection response, or cancer dependency. Rather than producing a black-box predictor alone, the group will compare mechanistic hypotheses: whether condensate emergence is best explained by intrinsic molecular grammar, cellular concentration and stoichiometry, interaction-network topology, post-translational regulation, or combinations of these factors. This project requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory has the breadth of expertise or coordination capacity to integrate high-content imaging, proteomics, structural bioinformatics, RNA biology, soft-matter physics, machine learning, and causal modeling at community scale. The proposed team would include molecular and cell biologists studying condensates, computational biologists, biophysicists, statisticians, imaging scientists, database curators, and trainees from research-intensive and primarily undergraduate institutions. NCEMS working-group meetings will enable consensus on metadata standards, benchmarking tasks, uncertainty reporting, and interpretable model evaluation. All code, workflows, harmonized metadata, trained models, and derived feature tables will be released under open licenses through reproducible containers and public repositories. Trainees will lead cross-institutional analysis modules, participate in data-integration hackathons, and receive training in open, team-based synthesis science. The expected outcomes are a reusable public atlas of condensate-associated molecular and cellular features, validated predictive models for emergent mesoscale organization, and testable hypotheses explaining how condensates convert molecular interactions into higher-order cellular phenotypes. By transforming fragmented public data into a coherent synthesis framework, this project will address a fundamental puzzle in cell biology and provide a community resource for predicting emergent organization across the molecular-to-cellular scale.

Biomolecular condensates exemplify mesoscale emergence: thousands of weak molecular interactions can collectively produce spatially organized, dynamic compartments that alter signaling, transcription, RNA metabolism, and stress responses without membrane boundaries. Yet a central unresolved question remains: when do molecular features such as intrinsic disorder, multivalency, post-translational modification, RNA binding, and interaction-network topology combine to generate a condensate state with predictable cellular consequences? This working group will synthesize public molecular, imaging, proteomic, and functional genomics data to derive generalizable rules linking molecular composition to emergent condensate behavior and downstream cellular phenotypes.

We will integrate existing datasets from Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Allen Cell Explorer, BioImage Archive, PRIDE, ProteomeXchange, ENCODE, DepMap, BioGRID, STRING, UniProt, AlphaFold, DisProt, PhosphoSitePlus, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, and publicly available single-cell transcriptomic and perturbation screens. The project will focus on human nuclear and cytoplasmic condensates involved in transcriptional regulation, RNA processing, DNA damage response, and stress adaptation. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, we will build a harmonized, open synthesis resource that connects protein sequence features, structural disorder, interaction valency, RNA association, post-translational modification, subcellular localization dynamics, cell-type context, and genetic dependency phenotypes.

The core scientific objective is to test whether condensate formation and functional impact can be predicted from multiscale public data better than from any individual data modality. We will develop interpretable machine-learning and network-based models to identify combinations of molecular features that distinguish constitutive condensate scaffolds, context-dependent clients, and disease-sensitive regulatory nodes. We will then ask how these mesoscale states map onto higher-order outcomes, including transcriptional programs, proliferation dependencies, stress resistance, and mutation-associated disease phenotypes. Particular emphasis will be placed on emergent properties that are not obvious from single-protein annotations, such as cooperative recruitment thresholds, modification-sensitive phase switching, and cell-type-specific condensate rewiring.

This project requires NCEMS support because it exceeds the capacity of a single laboratory: it demands coordinated expertise in cell biology, biophysics, proteomics, computational imaging, graph theory, machine learning, RNA biology, structural bioinformatics, and open-science software engineering. The working group will include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and national data-resource teams, with intentional participation by early-career scientists, graduate students, and postdoctoral fellows. NCEMS convening infrastructure will enable sustained cross-disciplinary synthesis, community standards for condensate data annotation, and collaborative benchmarking of computational models.

Deliverables will include an open Condensate Emergence Atlas; reproducible workflows for data harmonization, image-derived localization feature extraction, and multimodal modeling; benchmark datasets for predicting condensate membership and context-dependent function; and community-authored guidelines for integrating condensate-related public data. Trainees will participate in hackathons, model-building sprints, and team-science workshops focused on reproducible analysis, FAIR data practices, and responsible AI. By transforming fragmented public datasets into a coherent mesoscale synthesis framework, this project will address a fundamental question in molecular and cellular biology: how do distributed molecular interactions give rise to emergent cellular organization and function?

This Working Group will synthesize publicly available molecular, imaging, proteomic, genetic, and phenotypic datasets to answer a central question in emergence biology: what combinations of molecular features, cellular context, and network architecture give rise to condensates with distinct material properties and downstream cellular outcomes?
