Instead, it will integrate existing resources including LLPS and condensate databases, protein sequence and intrinsically disordered region annotations, post-translational modification datasets, protein interaction networks, public affinity-purification and proximity-labeling proteomics, microscopy image repositories, CRISPR and RNAi perturbation screens, single-cell transcriptomic atlases, and disease-variant databases. By linking molecular composition to mesoscale condensate behavior and cell-level phenotypes, the project will directly address NCEMS priorities in understanding emergent properties between biomolecules and organelles. The Working Group will develop an open, extensible Condensate Emergence Knowledge Graph connecting proteins, RNAs, modifications, interaction motifs, environmental conditions, localization patterns, condensate classes, and phenotypic consequences. This resource will support three analytical aims. First, we will identify conserved and context-specific molecular signatures that predict condensate formation across cell types and organisms, distinguishing drivers, clients, and regulators. Second, we will infer how multivalent interactions, disorder, RNA binding, charge patterning, and post-translational modification jointly shape emergent material states such as liquid-like dynamics, gelation, and solidification. Third, we will connect condensate state transitions to higher-order cellular outcomes, including stress response, transcriptional regulation, RNA metabolism, signaling, and neurodegenerative disease phenotypes. Methodologically, the team will combine network science, interpretable machine learning, causal discovery, natural-language mining of the literature, and computer vision applied to public microscopy images. A major innovation will be the development of benchmark datasets and transparent models that predict condensate behavior from molecular and contextual features while quantifying uncertainty and dataset bias. This synthesis effort requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory has the expertise or coordination capacity to harmonize heterogeneous public datasets spanning biophysics, cell biology, genomics, proteomics, imaging, and clinical genetics. The Working Group will include condensate biologists, protein biophysicists, RNA biologists, data scientists, image analysts, network theorists, and experts in open scientific software from diverse institutions and career stages. Trainees will participate through structured data-synthesis sprints, reproducible workflow workshops, cross-lab mentoring, and leadership roles in benchmark construction and software documentation. All products will follow open science principles: curated datasets, metadata standards, code, workflows, model outputs, and tutorials will be released through public repositories with persistent identifiers and community governance. The expected outcome is a predictive, community-validated framework for explaining how molecular-scale features generate mesoscale condensate properties and how those properties influence cellular function. This will transform a fragmented literature into a reusable synthesis platform, resolve long-standing debates about determinants of condensate specificity and pathological maturation, and train a new cohort of scientists in collaborative, data-intensive molecular and cellular biology.

No new experimental data will be generated.

The primary scientific objective is to determine whether emergent condensate behaviors can be predicted from combinations of molecular grammar, network context, and cellular state. Specifically, we will ask: (1) Which sequence, structural, and interaction features best distinguish condensates with liquid-like, gel-like, or solid-like behaviors? (2) How do post-translational modifications and RNA abundance shift mesoscale material states? (3) Which condensate properties are associated with downstream cellular phenotypes such as stress resilience, altered transcription, impaired translation, cytotoxicity, or disease vulnerability? (4) Are there conserved cross-organelle principles that explain why some condensates buffer cellular noise whereas others amplify pathological transitions?

Methodologically, the group will develop an open, reproducible computational framework combining ontology-driven data harmonization, probabilistic graphical models, multimodal representation learning, interpretable machine learning, and network-based causal discovery. A key deliverable will be a community-curated condensate knowledge graph linking molecules, interactions, condensate types, material properties, perturbations, cell states, and phenotypes. We will benchmark predictive models across independent datasets and prioritize interpretable rules rather than black-box correlations, enabling the field to evaluate proposed principles of condensate emergence.

This project requires NCEMS support because the necessary expertise and data integration exceed the scope of any single laboratory. The working group will bring together cell biologists, biophysicists, RNA biologists, proteomics experts, imaging scientists, computational biologists, machine-learning researchers, statisticians, database curators, and trainees from diverse institution types and geographic regions. NCEMS will provide the collaborative infrastructure needed to establish shared standards, resolve conflicting annotations, train early-career scientists in synthesis science, and produce community resources. All workflows, harmonized metadata schemas, analysis notebooks, models, and derived datasets will be released openly under FAIR principles. By transforming fragmented public data into testable rules of mesoscale organization, this project will address a fundamental question in molecular and cellular biology: how collective molecular interactions generate emergent compartments that shape cell fate.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates exemplify mesoscale emergence: dynamic assemblies arise from weak multivalent interactions among proteins, RNAs, and metabolites, yet produce new cellular properties such as spatial biochemical compartmentalization, stress adaptation, and disease-associated aggregation. Despite extensive public data on phase-separating proteins, RNA localization, proteomes, transcriptomes, live-cell imaging, and genetic perturbations, the field lacks a synthesis framework that predicts when molecular components collectively generate condensate behavior in specific cellular contexts. This working group will integrate existing public datasets to address a central question: which combinations of molecular features and cellular states are sufficient to predict the emergent formation, dissolution, material properties, and functional consequences of biomolecular condensates?

The project will synthesize publicly available data from phase-separation and condensate databases, Human Protein Atlas subcellular localization images, OpenCell protein localization measurements, BioImage Archive microscopy datasets, ENCODE and GEO transcriptomic profiles, PRIDE and ProteomeXchange proteomics, RNA-binding protein and RNA interactome datasets, intrinsically disordered region and low-complexity sequence annotations, post-translational modification resources, DepMap/CRISPR screens, Perturb-seq datasets, and published stress-granule, nucleolar, P-body, transcriptional condensate, and disease-aggregate studies. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, the group will harmonize metadata, develop interoperable ontologies for condensate identity and material state, and construct a multiscale knowledge graph linking molecular composition, sequence grammar, RNA abundance, post-translational regulation, imaging-derived mesoscale phenotypes, perturbation responses, and cellular outcomes.

We will develop open analytical strategies combining computer vision, network science, representation learning, causal inference, and biophysical modeling. Image foundation models will extract condensate features such as number, size distribution, morphology, coarsening behavior, and localization from public microscopy. Graph neural networks and interpretable statistical models will then test whether emergent condensate states can be predicted from molecular interaction potential, expression stoichiometry, RNA context, and perturbation history. Comparative analyses across cell types, stresses, developmental states, and disease models will identify generalizable principles and context-specific exceptions. A key deliverable will be a public “condensate emergence map” that predicts transitions among dispersed, liquid-like, gel-like, and aggregate-like states and links these transitions to downstream phenotypes including transcriptional regulation, translation repression, proteostasis, and cell viability.

This effort requires NCEMS support because it exceeds the scope of any single laboratory: it demands coordinated expertise in molecular biophysics, cell biology, RNA biology, proteomics, bioimage analysis, machine learning, ontology development, and open-science infrastructure. The working group will include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, national data repositories, and computational biology centers, with trainees embedded in cross-institutional analysis teams. Graduate students and postdocs will receive hands-on training through hackathons, reproducible workflow workshops, FAIR data curation sprints, and mentored team-authored publications.

All harmonized metadata, code, workflows, trained models, benchmark datasets, and interactive visualizations will be released openly under community-approved licenses using reproducible containers and version-controlled repositories. By transforming fragmented public observations into a predictive synthesis of condensate emergence, this project will provide mechanistic insight into how molecular-scale properties give rise to mesoscale cellular organization and higher-order cellular phenotypes.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates are mesoscale assemblies that emerge from multivalent molecular interactions and reorganize cellular biochemistry without membrane boundaries. Although thousands of proteins and RNAs have been implicated in condensates, a central puzzle remains unresolved: when do condensates act as adaptive organizers that buffer cellular stress, and when do they become amplifiers of dysfunction leading to altered signaling, growth, or disease phenotypes? This Working Group will synthesize publicly available molecular, imaging, proteomic, transcriptomic, and phenotypic datasets to identify generalizable principles linking condensate composition and material state to higher-order cellular outcomes.

The project will use only existing public data, integrating resources such as PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, CD-CODE, UniProt, AlphaFold structures, post-translational modification repositories, ENCODE and RNA-binding protein datasets, ProteomeXchange stress-response proteomics, Image Data Resource and BioImage Archive microscopy datasets, LINCS perturbational transcriptomics, DepMap fitness screens, and published high-content imaging screens. We will construct an open, versioned knowledge graph connecting condensate-associated proteins and RNAs to sequence features, predicted disorder, interaction valency, post-translational modifications, localization, microscopy-derived condensate morphology, stress conditions, pathway activity, and cellular phenotypes. Using interpretable machine learning, network modeling, and causal-inference strategies, we will test whether specific combinations of molecular features and network positions predict emergent condensate behaviors such as nucleation, fusion, hardening, reversibility, recruitment selectivity, and downstream effects on transcription, translation, signaling, and cell viability.

The central scientific question is whether mesoscale condensate properties can be predicted from integrated molecular features and, in turn, whether those properties explain cellular-scale outcomes better than the properties of individual molecules alone. This directly addresses emergence across scales: local molecular interactions give rise to condensate material states, which then reshape information flow, biochemical reaction organization, and cellular decisions. The project will also resolve a long-standing inconsistency in the field by harmonizing heterogeneous condensate annotations, imaging measurements, and experimental contexts into a shared ontology that distinguishes evidence for phase separation, clustering, aggregation, and functional compartmentalization.

NCEMS support is essential because the work exceeds the capacity of any single laboratory. The Working Group will bring together condensate biophysicists, cell biologists, RNA biologists, proteomics experts, bioimage analysts, data scientists, network theorists, ontology developers, and trainees from research-intensive universities, minority-serving institutions, and primarily undergraduate institutions. NCEMS will enable structured team science, dataset harmonization, cloud-based analysis, benchmark development, and community governance for open resources.

All outputs will follow open science principles: curated datasets, ontologies, code, workflows, trained models, documentation, and interactive visualization tools will be released publicly with reproducible computational environments. Trainees will participate in cross-disciplinary synthesis sprints, receive training in FAIR data practices, bioimage analysis, graph machine learning, and responsible AI, and co-lead benchmark challenges. The expected outcome is a community resource and predictive framework that transforms condensate biology from a catalog of components into a mechanistic, data-driven understanding of how mesoscale assemblies generate emergent cellular functions.

abstract_original: Membraneless ribonucleoprotein condensates such as stress granules, P-bodies, nucleoli, and nuclear speckles are archetypal mesoscale systems: they emerge from many weak molecular interactions yet shape translation, RNA fate, signaling, and cell survival. Despite extensive public data, the field lacks a unified, predictive framework explaining when specific RNAs and proteins form condensates, how condensate composition varies across cellular contexts, and which mesoscale properties causally associate with downstream cellular phenotypes. This working group will synthesize existing public datasets to answer a central question: what molecular, biophysical, and network features predict the emergent assembly, composition, dynamics, and cellular consequences of human RNP condensates? The project will integrate only publicly available data, including fluorescence imaging datasets from the Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Image Data Resource, Allen Cell Explorer, and published live-cell stress-granule studies; proteomic and interactome data from BioGRID, IntAct, AP-MS, proximity-labeling, and condensate-enrichment studies; RNA localization and RNA-protein interaction data from ENCODE, POSTAR, CLIP-seq, APEX-seq, and subcellular fractionation studies; perturbation and phenotype data from DepMap, genome-scale CRISPR screens, Perturb-seq, and drug-response repositories; and sequence-derived features such as intrinsically disordered regions, low-complexity domains, prion-like domains, charge patterning, RNA-binding motifs, post-translational modification sites, and predicted structures. The synthesis will produce a cross-scale atlas linking molecular features to mesoscale condensate behaviors and cellular outcomes. We will develop harmonized ontologies for condensate identity, experimental perturbation, stress condition, cell type, and measured mesoscale phenotype, then use computer vision to extract comparable features from public images, including condensate number, size distribution, shape, colocalization, dissolution kinetics, and spatial relationship to organelles. These features will be integrated with molecular interaction networks and perturbation phenotypes using interpretable graph machine learning, causal discovery, and physics-informed models of multivalent assembly. The goal is not simply to classify condensate components, but to identify generalizable rules explaining how emergent mesoscale properties arise from molecular composition and how these properties influence higher-order cell states such as translational arrest, antiviral response, proteostasis failure, and stress adaptation. This project requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory can assemble the needed expertise in condensate biology, RNA biology, proteomics, quantitative imaging, biophysics, machine learning, network science, and open-science infrastructure, nor can it coordinate the community standards required to make heterogeneous public data interoperable. The working group will include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, data science centers, and experimental condensate laboratories, with active roles for graduate students and postdoctoral fellows. Trainees will participate in reproducible workflow development, image-analysis hackathons, model benchmarking, and community annotation jamborees. All outputs will be open: curated datasets, metadata standards, analysis notebooks, trained models, uncertainty estimates, and interactive visualizations will be released through public repositories. The expected outcome is a reusable predictive framework for mesoscale emergence in RNP condensates, providing testable hypotheses for the broader community and a model for synthesis-driven discovery in molecular and cellular biology.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates are a central example of emergence in molecular and cellular biology: multivalent interactions among proteins and RNAs generate mesoscale compartments whose properties cannot be inferred from any single component alone. Yet a long-standing puzzle remains unresolved: why do some molecular assemblies reproducibly form functional condensates in living cells, while compositionally similar systems remain diffuse, aggregate pathologically, or reorganize only under specific cellular states? This Working Group will synthesize publicly available data to derive generalizable rules linking molecular features, interaction networks, cellular context, and emergent condensate behavior. The project will integrate existing datasets spanning scales: protein sequence features and low-complexity domains from UniProt and AlphaFold; protein-protein and protein-RNA interaction networks from BioGRID, STRING, ENCODE, eCLIP, and POSTAR; subcellular localization and protein abundance from the Human Protein Atlas and OpenCell; perturbation and morphology profiles from Cell Painting, LINCS, and image repositories such as the BioImage Archive and Image Data Resource; and transcriptomic and stress-response datasets from GEO, SRA, and single-cell atlases. No new experimental data will be generated. The central scientific question is: what combinations of molecular grammar, interaction topology, expression stoichiometry, and cellular state predict the emergence, material behavior, and functional consequences of mesoscale condensates? To address this, the team will build an open, harmonized condensate knowledge graph linking molecular components to imaging phenotypes, perturbations, disease associations, and cell-state variables. We will develop interpretable machine-learning models and causal network analyses to identify thresholds and nonlinear interactions that distinguish functional condensate formation from non-condensing assemblies or pathological aggregates. A major analytical innovation will be the integration of foundation-model-derived image embeddings with molecular interaction and sequence embeddings, allowing condensate-like mesoscale phenotypes to be compared across cell types, perturbations, laboratories, and imaging modalities. The project requires NCEMS support because it exceeds the capacity of any single laboratory: it demands coordinated expertise in cell biology, phase separation biophysics, RNA biology, proteomics, microscopy, artificial intelligence, statistics, network science, and open-science software engineering. The Working Group will include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and national data-resource centers, with graduate students and postdoctoral fellows embedded in all stages of data curation, model development, reproducibility assessment, and community dissemination. Training activities will include hands-on workshops in FAIR data integration, reproducible workflow construction, biological image analysis, and responsible AI for molecular and cellular synthesis. Expected products include a public condensate data atlas, reproducible computational pipelines, benchmark datasets for predicting condensate emergence, interactive visualization tools, and community guidelines for annotating mesoscale cellular structures from heterogeneous public data. By synthesizing diverse existing datasets, this project will generate testable principles for how molecular-scale interactions give rise to emergent mesoscale cellular organization and how those mesoscale states influence cellular phenotypes. The resulting framework will advance fundamental understanding of cellular organization, provide reusable infrastructure for the broader community, and establish a model for open, collaborative synthesis research in emergent molecular and cellular systems.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates are a central example of mesoscale emergence: weak molecular interactions among proteins, RNAs, and chromatin can collectively generate dynamic compartments with properties not predictable from any single component. Yet a long-standing puzzle remains unresolved: why do some predicted phase-separating molecules form functional condensates in cells, while others do not, and when do condensates become pathological or phenotypically consequential? This working group will synthesize publicly available molecular and cellular datasets to develop a generalizable, data-driven framework linking molecular features to emergent condensate behavior and downstream cellular outcomes. The project will integrate existing resources including human and model-organism proteomes, intrinsically disordered region annotations, post-translational modification databases, RNA-binding and protein interaction maps, public proximity-labeling datasets, single-cell and bulk transcriptomic atlases, high-content microscopy repositories, CRISPR perturbation screens, disease variant catalogs, and curated condensate databases such as PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, and RNA granule resources. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, the working group will harmonize heterogeneous datasets into an open, versioned knowledge graph describing condensate-associated molecules, their biophysical features, interaction contexts, cellular locations, perturbation responses, and phenotype associations. We will address three linked questions: (1) What combinations of molecular features and cellular context best predict condensate membership and mesoscale compartment identity? (2) Which emergent properties, such as compositional buffering, stress responsiveness, spatial co-localization, and dynamic exchange, can be inferred by integrating public imaging, proteomic, and perturbation data? (3) Which condensate states are associated with higher-order cellular outcomes, including stress tolerance, altered gene regulation, neurodegeneration-related toxicity, and cancer cell fitness? Analytically, the group will combine graph machine learning, interpretable multimodal models, causal inference from perturbation screens, and image-derived phenotype embeddings. A major methodological deliverable will be an open benchmark for condensate prediction and emergent-property inference, including negative controls, uncertainty estimates, and reproducible workflows. This synthesis requires NCEMS support because the necessary expertise spans biophysics, cell biology, RNA biology, microscopy, proteomics, machine learning, knowledge engineering, and open-science infrastructure, and because the data integration challenge exceeds the scope of any single laboratory. The working group will deliberately include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, national data repositories, and international open-data communities, with participation from graduate students and postdoctoral fellows as core analysts. Trainees will receive hands-on training through hackathons, reproducibility clinics, FAIR data curation sprints, and team-based manuscript and software development. All outputs, including harmonized metadata, analysis notebooks, trained models, benchmark datasets, and visualization tools, will be released publicly under permissive licenses with community governance. By transforming fragmented public datasets into a coherent synthesis framework, this project will provide mechanistic insight into how molecular interactions produce emergent mesoscale organization and how that organization shapes cellular phenotype.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless organelles formed via liquid-liquid phase separation—represent a paradigm-shifting example of mesoscale emergence in cellular biology. These dynamic assemblies bridge the critical gap between individual biomolecules and membrane-bound organelles, orchestrating essential cellular functions ranging from gene regulation to stress response. However, despite an exponential increase in individual laboratory studies, the universal biophysical rules and stoichiometric conditions that dictate the unexpected emergence of these mesoscale structures remain a long-standing mystery. Furthermore, predicting how localized condensate dynamics influence global, higher-order cellular outcomes remains beyond current capabilities. This gap in knowledge persists largely because existing experimental data—ranging from atomic-resolution structural biophysics to whole-cell spatial transcriptomics and high-content imaging—are highly siloed across disparate public repositories.

To address this, we propose the establishment of the "Meso-Condensate Synthesis Working Group" (MCS-WG), a transdisciplinary collaborative initiative designed to synthesize existing multimodal public datasets to decode the emergent properties of biomolecular condensates. By integrating fragmented data from PRIDE (mass spectrometry proteomics), GEO (transcriptomics), PhaSepDB (phase separation curation), AlphaFold Protein Structure Database (structural conformations), and the Image Data Resource (high-content cellular microscopy), our team will construct a massive, multi-scale biological knowledge graph. Crucially, this project will rely entirely on publicly available data, generating no new experimental data, thereby directly answering the NCEMS call for community-scale synthesis.

Our working group will leverage advanced Artificial Intelligence (AI), specifically geometric deep learning and multi-modal graph neural networks, to identify hidden patterns that drive mesoscale phase separation. Our research objectives are threefold: (1) Answer novel questions regarding the evolutionary conservation of disordered protein regions and their emergent phase-separation behaviors across distinct cellular stress states; (2) Solve the long-standing puzzle of how varied macromolecular concentrations dynamically trigger mesoscale assembly and disassembly; and (3) Develop an innovative, open-source AI analytical framework that predicts subcellular phenotypic outcomes based on molecular-level perturbations.

The complexity of this synthesis requires the unique support and resources of NCEMS, as it extends far beyond the computational or domain expertise of any single laboratory. The MCS-WG will assemble a diverse team of structural biophysicists, cellular biologists, data ontologists, and machine learning experts from varied geographic locations and institutional tiers. In strong alignment with NCEMS goals, our initiative places a heavy emphasis on workforce development. We will actively recruit and cross-train early-career researchers (graduate students and postdocs) from historically underrepresented backgrounds, equipping them with a dual skill set in molecular biology and advanced data science. Furthermore, committing strictly to open science principles, all curated datasets, harmonized ontologies, AI model architectures, and analysis pipelines will be released publicly via open-access community portals, ensuring reproducibility and providing a lasting resource for the molecular and cellular biosciences community. Through this transdisciplinary synthesis, we will unravel how mesoscale emergence dictates cellular fate.

These membraneless compartments organize biochemical reactions dynamically, yet bridging the gap between nanoscale molecular interactions and their mesoscale architectural properties remains a critical challenge. This highly collaborative, transdisciplinary team will synthesize entirely publicly available datasets to decipher the rules governing emergent properties of biomolecular condensates. The project is structured around three core synthesis objectives: (1) Map the molecular grammar of IDPs and associated post-translational modifications to mesoscale emergent properties such as condensate viscosity, critical concentration thresholds, and multiphase spatial architecture; (2) Link these emergent mesoscale features directly to cellular-level outcomes, specifically focusing on stress granule dynamics and neurodegenerative protein aggregation pathways; and (3) Develop open-source predictive algorithms capable of inferring higher-order cellular phenotypes strictly from primary molecular sequences and available interactome topologies. The MCC Working Group will recruit diverse computational and biological scientists, intentionally embedding postdoctoral researchers and graduate students into the core data science workflows. This will provide unprecedented training opportunities, actively cultivating a data-savvy, next-generation workforce fluent in cross-disciplinary AI and biological synthesis. Furthermore, our initiative commits rigorously to community-created open science policies. abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates represent a quintessential example of mesoscale emergence, where transient, multivalent interactions among thousands of biomolecules spontaneously give rise to highly organized, functional, membrane-less organelles. These mesoscale structures dictate critical subcellular outcomes, ranging from stress adaptation to gene regulation. However, the precise rules governing how molecular-level features—such as intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), RNA secondary structures, and post-translational modifications (PTMs)—dynamically scale to produce emergent mesoscale physical properties remain a long-standing puzzle in cellular biology. Despite the exponential growth of publicly available transcriptomic, proteomic, structural, and spatial imaging datasets, these rich resources remain deeply siloed across disparate repositories. Addressing this complex emergent phenomenon requires a community-scale data synthesis approach that far exceeds the computational and disciplinary capabilities of any individual research laboratory.

We propose the establishment of the Condensate Emergence Synthesis (CES) Working Group to decode the multiscale grammar of condensate formation. This transdisciplinary team will unite domain experts in artificial intelligence, computational biophysics, cell biology, and multi-omics. Adhering strictly to the NCEMS mandate, we will generate no new experimental data. Instead, we will synthesize massive public datasets, including molecular interaction networks (BioGRID), structural and disorder profiles (AlphaFold DB, DisProt), high-throughput proteomics (PRIDE), and mesoscale spatial imaging (Image Data Resource, Allen Cell Atlas). 

Our primary scientific objective is to develop an innovative, multimodal Graph Neural Network (GNN) framework to uncover the hidden principles of mesoscale emergence. We will address a novel question: How do heterogeneous molecular inputs synergistically trigger the spatiotemporal emergence of specific condensates, such as stress granules, under shifting environmental pressures? By harmonizing these disparate, multi-scale data streams into a unified, dynamic knowledge graph, our AI-driven analytical strategy will predict how distinct molecular perturbations cascade upward to alter mesoscale properties—such as condensate size, viscosity, and composition—and ultimately influence cellular phenotypes.

Executing this transdisciplinary integration fundamentally relies on the unique infrastructure, computational resources, and collaborative ecosystem provided by NCEMS. By bringing together diverse scientific perspectives across career stages and institutional levels, we will translate fragmented biological data into a cohesive understanding of subcellular emergence. 

Crucially, the CES Working Group will adhere strictly to community-created open science policies. All integrated databases, AI models, and reproducible analytical pipelines will be distributed through open-source repositories following FAIR principles. Furthermore, this initiative will provide unparalleled training opportunities for a diverse cohort of graduate students and postdoctoral researchers. Through intensive, cross-disciplinary co-mentorship in advanced data science and systems biology, we will empower the future data-savvy workforce required to solve the next generation of biological mysteries.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates, such as stress granules and nucleoli, represent a quintessential example of emergent properties at the mesoscale. Arising from the dynamic, multivalent interactions of proteins and RNA, these membraneless organelles bridge the gap between individual biomolecules and higher-order cellular functions. Despite their critical roles in cellular organization, stress adaptation, and disease pathogenesis, the fundamental rules dictating how physical interactions at the atomic and molecular levels scale up to govern mesoscale condensation and macroscopic cellular phenotypes remain a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biosciences. Current biological research often captures these phenomena in isolated silos—producing disparate datasets on molecular structure, pairwise protein-protein interactions, or cellular imaging—leaving a critical knowledge gap in bridging these temporal and spatial dimensions.

To address this fundamental question of emergence, our Working Group proposes a community-scale synthesis of publicly available biological data to decode the mesoscale properties of biomolecular condensates. We will systematically integrate structural and sequence data (AlphaFold DB, DisProt, PDB), high-throughput interaction and proximity labeling networks (BioGRID, IntAct, PRIDE), transcriptomic profiles under distinct cellular stress states (GEO, SRA), and high-resolution spatial imaging data (Image Data Resource, EMPIAR). Crucially, this project will rely entirely on existing public data and will not generate any new experimental outputs.

Leveraging advanced artificial intelligence and data science, specifically multi-modal Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and contrastive representation learning, we will develop an innovative analytical strategy to fuse these disparate, multi-scale data types. Our primary objective is to construct 'Mesoscale-CondensateNet,' a predictive foundation model that mathematically maps how molecular grammars (such as intrinsically disordered regions, amino acid spacing, and interaction valencies) dictate emergent mesoscale properties (including droplet formation, material state transitions, and biochemical partitioning) and their subsequent cellular outcomes like gene regulation and stress survival.

This ambitious synthesis project fundamentally exceeds the capacity of any single laboratory or existing collaboration. It necessitates the specialized resources, computational infrastructure, and collaborative environment provided by NCEMS. We have assembled a transdisciplinary team encompassing structural biophysicists, cellular biologists, AI/machine learning experts, and data ontologists. This diverse partnership deliberately bridges multiple geographic locations, career stages, and institutional types to ensure a breadth of scientific perspectives.

Committed to gold-standard open science principles, all curated multimodal datasets, AI architectures, and reproducible analytical workflows will be openly shared via GitHub and Zenodo, strictly adhering to FAIR data practices. Furthermore, this working group will serve as a premier training incubator for the future data-savvy workforce. Through dedicated hackathons and cross-disciplinary mentorship, graduate students and postdoctoral trainees will be cross-trained at the cutting edge of artificial intelligence and mesoscale biology. Ultimately, this synthesis will solve a critical mystery in molecular biology, providing a transformative, open-access computational framework to predict condensate-driven emergent behaviors across the cellular landscape.

abstract_original:
The emergence of mesoscale biological structures—those bridging the gap between individual biomolecules and functional organelles—represents a fundamental frontier in the molecular and cellular biosciences. Biomolecular condensates, dynamic membraneless organelles formed via liquid-liquid phase separation, are paradigm examples of mesoscale emergence. While they critically regulate cellular outcomes such as stress response and gene expression, the principles dictating how 1D molecular sequences and local physical interactions collectively scale into complex, emergent 3D mesoscale behaviors remain a long-standing puzzle. The global research community has generated massive, yet deeply siloed, datasets spanning protein sequences, interactomics, biophysical measurements, and subcellular imaging. Addressing the complexity of mesoscale phase separation far exceeds the capacity of any single research group, necessitating a transdisciplinary, community-scale data synthesis approach.

We propose the establishment of the 'Condensate Emergence Synthesis and Analytics' (CESA) Working Group to decode the multiscale rules of mesoscale condensate emergence. Strictly leveraging existing, publicly available data without generating new experimental datasets, this project will integrate sequence and structural databases (e.g., DisProt, AlphaFold DB), biophysical phase separation repositories (e.g., PhaSePro, CD-CODE), massive-scale stress-response proteomics (PRIDE, BioGRID), and high-resolution microscopy datasets from the Image Data Resource (IDR). 

To synthesize these highly heterogeneous modalities, our diverse team will develop innovative artificial intelligence and data science analytical strategies. Specifically, we will utilize multimodal Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and spatio-temporal deep learning to build predictive models. These models will map the continuum from molecular-level features (e.g., intrinsic disorder, valency) to mesoscale emergent properties (e.g., condensate viscosity, complex assembly/disassembly kinetics) and ultimately to cellular phenotypic outcomes, such as cellular resilience to environmental stress. 

This initiative heavily relies on the collaborative infrastructure provided by NCEMS. The CESA Working Group will convene a diverse assembly of experts, including molecular biophysicists, cell biologists, computational biologists, and AI/ML engineers. Our team is strategically assembled to reflect a broad spectrum of career stages, geographic locations, and institutional research levels (including primarily undergraduate and minority-serving institutions), ensuring diverse scientific perspectives.

A cornerstone of our proposal is the rigorous training of the next-generation, data-savvy scientific workforce. Graduate students and postdoctoral trainees embedded within the Working Group will undergo intensive cross-training at the intersection of molecular cell biology and advanced computational data synthesis, gaining essential, highly translatable skills in AI-driven biology.

Adhering strictly to Open Science principles, all synthesized datasets, AI architectures, analytical workflows, and educational materials will be made publicly accessible via FAIR-compliant repositories (e.g., Zenodo, GitHub) and disseminated through an interactive, community-facing web portal. By synthesizing disparate public data to map the continuous trajectory from molecular biophysics to emergent mesoscale architecture, the CESA Working Group will solve critical mysteries of cellular emergence, provide the community with transformative open-source analytical tools, and establish a new paradigm for transdisciplinary discovery in the biosciences.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates, formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), represent a quintessential example of biological emergence at the mesoscale. These dynamic, membrane-less compartments bridge individual molecular interactions—specifically between intrinsically disordered proteins and RNAs—with organelle-level organization and cellular-scale outcomes. During environmental stress, condensates such as stress granules rapidly emerge to protect cellular viability. However, a fundamental long-standing puzzle remains: what are the universal, emergent rules governing how molecular-scale perturbations collectively propagate to alter mesoscale condensate properties and subsequent global cellular responses? Currently, the molecular and cellular sciences are rich with fragmented data concerning condensate formation. Massive, publicly available repositories house transcriptomic and proteomic profiles of stress responses (GEO, PRIDE), high-resolution microscopy of cellular compartments (Image Data Resource), and structural predictions of intrinsically disordered regions (AlphaFoldDB, DisProt). Yet, deciphering the emergent properties of these mesoscale structures is beyond the capability of any single research laboratory. It requires the community-scale synthesis of these disparate datasets using advanced artificial intelligence and transdisciplinary expertise. To address this compelling scientific question, our proposed NCEMS Working Group will synthesize diverse, publicly available multi-omics, structural, and high-content imaging datasets to uncover the rules of mesoscale emergence in stress condensates. We will develop a novel, AI-driven computational framework that integrates molecular sequence and structural disorder data with cellular-level phenotypic imaging. By employing multimodal Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and computer vision algorithms, we will map multi-scale relationships, identifying the precise biophysical thresholds where atomic and molecular interactions collectively trigger mesoscale phase transitions. Our project is defined by three primary objectives. First, we will construct a comprehensive, open-access multi-scale knowledge graph unifying public molecular, interaction, and cellular imaging data related to cellular stress states. Second, we will leverage machine learning to extract hidden physicochemical rules governing how emergent mesoscale networks dynamically reconfigure in response to distinct stressors. Third, we will develop predictive models linking mesoscale condensate behavior to macro-cellular fate. This synthesis necessitates the unique collaborative environment and computational resources provided by NCEMS. Our team brings together a diverse array of experts—spanning biophysics, structural biology, machine learning, and cellular imaging—from multiple geographic regions, career stages, and institutional research levels. Crucially, this initiative relies entirely on existing public data, requiring no new experimental generation. In strict adherence to open science principles, all integrated datasets, AI models, and analytical workflows will be publicly distributed following FAIR guidelines, ensuring complete reproducibility. Furthermore, this working group will serve as a premier training ground for the future data-savvy workforce. Graduate students and postdoctoral fellows will be integrated into the core leadership of the analytical subgroups, receiving cross-disciplinary mentorship in AI-driven data synthesis, biophysics, and reproducible team science. Ultimately, this collaborative effort will resolve critical mysteries regarding mesoscale biological emergence, catalyzing a paradigm shift in how we understand subcellular organization through the lens of big data.

abstract_original: The emergence of biomolecular condensates—membraneless organelles formed via liquid-liquid phase separation—represents a profound paradigm shift in our understanding of mesoscale cellular organization. Bridging the critical spatial gap between individual biomolecules and functional membrane-bound organelles, these condensates regulate vital cellular processes, notably stress responses, RNA metabolism, and gene expression. Despite the recent explosion of isolated experimental datasets, a unified understanding of how nanometer-scale interactions of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and nucleic acids collectively drive the emergence of micrometer-scale mesoscopic phenotypes remains a major, unresolved puzzle in molecular and cellular biosciences. Currently, vast amounts of heterogeneous, publicly available data exist in isolated silos: sequence-level IDP annotations (DisProt), large-scale proteomic profiles of isolated condensates (PRIDE), high-resolution structural predictions (AlphaFold DB), and mesoscale live-cell imaging datasets mapping spatial dynamics (BioImage Archive). No single research laboratory possesses the computational infrastructure, diverse domain knowledge, or cross-disciplinary expertise required to harmonize these multi-modal, multi-scale datasets. Addressing this fundamental gap necessitates a community-scale data synthesis approach, aligning perfectly with the core mission of NCEMS. We propose a transdisciplinary Working Group to integrate disparate multi-omic, structural, biophysical, and spatial imaging datasets to decode the fundamental physicochemical rules governing condensate emergence. By leveraging advanced artificial intelligence and data science methodologies, specifically multi-modal graph neural networks (GNNs) and deep representation learning, we will synthesize over 50,000 publicly available records spanning from the molecular to the cellular scale. Our collaborative synthesis project will address three compelling scientific questions: (1) What are the universal sequence and structural grammar rules that dictate multi-component, mesoscale condensate assembly? (2) How do emergent mesoscale biophysical properties, such as viscoelasticity and surface tension, arise predictably from the dynamic interactome of IDPs? and (3) How do these emergent mesoscale network properties dictate global cellular phenotypes, particularly cellular survival and adaptation during environmental stress? Crucially, this project will rely exclusively on the rigorous synthesis of existing public data, generating no new experimental data, but rather pioneering an innovative, AI-driven analytical framework for mesoscale biology. To achieve this, our Working Group convenes a diverse, multi-institutional collaborative team encompassing molecular biophysicists, structural biologists, AI/ML data scientists, and cell physiologists. This team spans early-career and established investigators from R1 institutions, Primarily Undergraduate Institutions (PUIs), and historically underrepresented institutions, ensuring a wide array of scientific perspectives and geographic diversity. Deeply committed to open science principles, our team will ensure all integrated datasets, trained AI models, and analytical workflows are disseminated through public repositories (e.g., GitHub, Zenodo) using reproducible, containerized pipelines. Furthermore, this initiative is highly dedicated to training the future data-savvy workforce. We will actively fund and integrate graduate students and postdoctoral researchers into the collaborative research efforts. Through specialized 'synthesis hackathons,' structured peer-mentorship networks, and intensive cross-training at the intersection of AI and molecular biophysics, we will equip early-career researchers with the transdisciplinary computational skills required to lead the next generation of emergence-focused biological synthesis research.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates, formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), represent a quintessential example of emergent phenomena at the mesoscale. These membraneless organelles dynamically assemble from interacting networks of proteins and nucleic acids, fundamentally bridging the gap between individual biomolecules and complex subcellular organization. While recent years have seen an explosion of publicly available data on LLPS—ranging from intrinsic disorder profiles and high-throughput proteomics to live-cell imaging and mutational databases—these datasets remain heavily siloed across disparate platforms. Consequently, a long-standing puzzle remains: How do the sequence-level 'grammars' of thousands of distinct molecules interact collectively to drive the emergent biophysical properties of mesoscale condensates, and how do perturbations in these systems cascade into cellular dysfunction? 

To address this compelling question, we propose the 'Condensate Emergence Synthesis Network' (CESN), a multidisciplinary Working Group designed to synthesize massive, heterogeneous public datasets using advanced artificial intelligence (AI) and data science. Our transdisciplinary team unites experts in computational biophysics, structural biology, multi-omics, machine learning, and cell biology. By integrating protein structure and disorder databases (e.g., AlphaFold DB, DisProt), phase separation repositories (PhaSepDB, CD-CODE), large-scale interactomes (BioGRID), and clinical genomic datasets (ClinVar, TCGA), we will develop a unified, open-source computational framework. 

Our project will employ Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and multimodal deep learning to construct a predictive multi-scale model of condensate emergence. We aim to (1) define the molecular and thermodynamic rules governing the co-partitioning of multi-component mesoscale assemblies, (2) predict the emergent biophysical states of these condensates under varying cellular stress conditions, and (3) map how disease-associated mutations disrupt mesoscale homeostasis to drive pathological cellular phenotypes, such as neurodegeneration and oncogenesis. 

This community-scale synthesis project uniquely aligns with the NCEMS mission. It generates no new experimental data but rather extracts unprecedented value from existing repositories, a task computationally and intellectually beyond the scope of any single laboratory. The working group will leverage NCEMS resources to facilitate intensive, cross-disciplinary collaboration among researchers from diverse geographic, career-stage, and institutional backgrounds. 

Furthermore, this initiative places a strong emphasis on workforce development and open science. We will integrate graduate students and postdoctoral researchers as core drivers of the project, providing them with essential cross-training at the critical intersection of AI, big data management, and mesoscale biology. All integrated databases, machine learning pipelines, and analytical workflows will be rigorously documented and released through open-access portals following FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data principles. Ultimately, this synthesis effort will not only solve fundamental mysteries regarding mesoscale biological emergence but also establish innovative analytical strategies and cultivate a data-savvy workforce poised to lead the next generation of molecular and cellular sciences.

While massive amounts of experimental data exist detailing the intrinsic disorder of individual proteins, in vitro biophysical properties, and phenomenological cellular imaging, a fundamental gap remains in understanding how molecular sequence grammar and dynamic cellular microenvironments integrate to predictably dictate the emergent material properties of these condensates. A critical, long-standing puzzle in cellular biology is how these finely tuned mesoscale phase transitions occasionally fail, leading to irreversible, aberrant aggregates associated with neurodegenerative diseases. Unraveling this multiscale complexity is beyond the computational and domain-specific capabilities of any single research laboratory. The NCEMS infrastructure is essential not only for the logistical facilitation of intensive, hybrid synthesis meetings critical for cross-pollinating ideas among distinct disciplines, but also for standardizing community-scale data fusion. Using exclusively existing, publicly available data, our team will build an open-source data integration pipeline that harmonizes molecular features (e.g., intrinsically disordered regions, valency, post-translational modifications) with spatial proteomics and quantitative live-cell imaging metrics. Our AI-driven models will predict how specific microenvironmental shifts (such as localized pH changes, molecular crowding, and ATP fluctuations) trigger mesoscale phase transitions, mapping the precise trajectory from monomeric proteins to functional mesoscale assemblies, and ultimately to higher-order cellular stress resilience. By synthesizing siloed data to map the emergence of mesoscale properties, this project will answer novel questions about subcellular organization, pioneer innovative computational strategies, and provide an unparalleled collaborative training environment.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates, formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), represent a quintessential example of emergence at the mesoscale. Bridging the critical gap between individual interacting biomolecules and higher-order cellular organization, these membraneless organelles dynamically partition proteins and nucleic acids to regulate essential cellular outcomes, from stress adaptation to gene expression. Despite an explosion of publicly available data characterizing intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs), protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks, and phenotypic stress responses, a fundamental, long-standing puzzle remains: How do atomic and molecular-level 'grammars' predictably encode the emergent biophysical properties of mesoscale condensates, and how do these mesoscale structures subsequently dictate macroscopic cellular phenotypes? Solving this requires a scale of data synthesis and computational modeling far beyond the capability of any individual laboratory.

This Working Group proposes a community-scale synthesis project to decipher the rules of mesoscale emergence in biomolecular condensates using artificial intelligence (AI) and multi-scale data integration. By uniting a diverse, transdisciplinary team of biophysicists, computational biologists, AI/machine learning experts, and cell biologists from multiple institutions across varying research levels, we will integrate heterogeneous public datasets. Specifically, we will synthesize biophysical condensate databases (e.g., PhaSepDB, CD-CODE, DisProt), multi-omic profiles from GEO and PRIDE (transcriptomics and proteomics under cellular stress), and structural interactome data (AlphaFold-DB, PDB). We will not generate new experimental data; instead, we will leverage these vast repositories to develop innovative AI architectures, including sequence-to-function Large Language Models (LLMs) and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs).

Our project has three distinct aims: (1) Synthesize molecular and biophysical datasets to construct a unified knowledge graph of condensate-forming proteins and their emergent physicochemical properties (e.g., viscosity, critical concentration thresholds). (2) Develop AI-driven analytical strategies to predict mesoscale condensate emergence based solely on input molecular features and environmental cellular conditions. (3) Map these emergent mesoscale properties to higher-order cellular outcomes by integrating stress-response transcriptomic and proteomic data, uncovering how condensate dynamics drive cellular survival and adaptation.

Crucially, this Working Group relies on the unique infrastructure and collaborative environment provided by NCEMS to foster cross-disciplinary synergy. The project will actively train the next generation of data-savvy scientists by embedding graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in a collaborative, team-science environment. Trainees will lead specific cross-disciplinary integration tasks and participate in data-science bootcamps, acquiring highly sought-after skills at the intersection of AI and biology. Furthermore, we are deeply committed to Open Science principles; all curated datasets, predictive models, and analytical pipelines will be made freely available to the community via open-access repositories (e.g., GitHub, Zenodo) using reproducible workflows. Ultimately, this synthesis will not only resolve critical mysteries regarding mesoscale biological organization but will also provide the broader scientific community with groundbreaking open-source tools to predict emergent cellular phenomena.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates, formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), represent a quintessential example of mesoscale emergence in biology. These dynamic, non-membrane-bound organelles assemble from individual macromolecules to exhibit entirely new collective properties—such as tunable viscosity, selective permeability, and spatially restricted biochemical reactions. They effectively bridge the gap between single biomolecules and higher-order cellular phenotypes. Despite an explosion of single-lab experimental studies, the universal sequence grammar, biophysical parameters, and thermodynamic thresholds governing this mesoscale emergence across space and time remain a long-standing puzzle. Furthermore, predicting how these mesoscale properties dictate macro-cellular behaviors, such as survival mechanisms during cellular stress, is currently beyond the computational and analytical capacity of any individual research group.

To address this critical gap, we propose the Working Group 'Condensome-AI', a transdisciplinary team comprising structural biologists, biophysicists, machine learning experts, and cell biologists. We will leverage artificial intelligence and advanced data science methodologies to synthesize massive, publicly available, yet currently siloed datasets. Specifically, we will integrate biophysical droplet databases (e.g., PhaSePro, LLPSDB), high-resolution structural predictions (AlphaFold, PDB), global interactome datasets (BioGRID, PRIDE), and high-throughput cellular imaging repositories (Human Protein Atlas, Image Data Resource). In strict adherence to NCEMS guidelines, this project will generate no new experimental data. Instead, it relies entirely on community-scale synthesis to construct a unified, predictive framework for mesoscale emergence.

Our project pursues three core scientific objectives: (1) Answer the novel question of how combinations of intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) and structured RNA-binding domains synergize to govern emergent rheological properties across different metabolic states; (2) Solve the long-standing mystery of how shifts in environmental energy and molecular composition trigger the sudden spatial and temporal appearance of these mesoscale structures; and (3) Develop 'MesoPredict,' an innovative, AI-driven analytical pipeline utilizing graph neural networks to predict condensate composition and subsequent cellular impacts directly from omics profiles.

Executing this synthesis requires the unique infrastructure and collaborative support of NCEMS. By bringing together diverse talent from distinct geographic locations and institutional tiers, we will foster a research environment impossible within traditional single-discipline grants. Our partnership emphasizes diversity and mentorship, deliberately pairing senior computational scientists with biology-focused graduate students and postdoctoral researchers. Through specialized computational bootcamps and collaborative working group sessions, we will actively train a data-savvy, next-generation workforce capable of navigating the intersection of AI and biological emergence.

Finally, our Working Group is deeply committed to rigorous open science practices. All synthesized datasets, AI/ML models, analytical workflows, and resultant code will be heavily documented, open-source, and distributed via community repositories like Zenodo and GitHub following FAIR data principles. By deciphering the complex language of mesoscale condensate emergence, this NCEMS-supported synthesis will fundamentally advance our understanding of cellular organization and provide a transformative, accessible resource for the entire molecular and cellular biosciences community.

abstract_original:
The emergence of mesoscale structures from nanoscale molecular interactions represents a fundamental frontier in the cellular biosciences. Among the most enigmatic of these phenomena are biomolecular condensates—membraneless organelles formed via liquid-liquid phase separation. While condensates are critical for compartmentalizing cellular processes and mediating stress responses, a long-standing puzzle remains: how do specific, dynamically changing combinations of proteins and nucleic acids predictably self-assemble into mesoscale structures with distinct biophysical properties, and how do these emergent properties dictate higher-order cellular phenotypes? Understanding this mesoscale emergence requires shifting from reductionist studies of individual proteins to a holistic, systems-level integration of molecular data.

To address this, we propose the establishment of the Meso-Condensate Synthesis Working Group, a transdisciplinary initiative dedicated to decoding the rules governing emergent condensate formation. Crucially, this project will generate no new experimental data; instead, it will leverage the unprecedented wealth of publicly available multi-modal data. We will synthesize and integrate sequence and AI-predicted structural features (AlphaFold DB, PDB), high-throughput transcriptomic and proteomic data mapping varied cellular states (GEO, PRIDE), molecular interaction networks (BioGRID, STRING), and curated phase-separation databases (PhaSepDB, CD-CODE).

Integrating these disparate, vast datasets to predict mesoscale physical chemistry is well beyond the computational and biological capabilities of any single laboratory, making NCEMS support essential. Our Working Group unites diverse experts—machine learning scientists, computational biophysicists, structural biologists, and molecular geneticists—spanning R1 institutions, primarily undergraduate institutions (PUIs), and historically black colleges and universities (HBCUs). This inclusive collaboration guarantees a broad geographic and career-stage distribution, ensuring diverse scientific perspectives.

Methodologically, we will utilize advanced artificial intelligence and data science techniques, specifically multi-layer graph neural networks (GNNs) and large language models adapted for proteins, to map state-dependent molecular interactomes. By synthesizing these datasets, we aim to answer novel questions: Can we predict the threshold concentrations and environmental triggers required for phase separation in vivo across varying cellular stress states? How do subtle genetic variations propagate through interaction networks to alter the emergent biophysical properties of these mesoscale droplets?

In strict adherence to open science principles, all integrated datasets, AI models, and analysis pipelines will be shared publicly via specialized open-science repositories, establishing gold-standard, reproducible workflows for the scientific community. Furthermore, this project strongly emphasizes training the future data-savvy workforce. Graduate students and postdoctoral trainees will be fully integrated into the Working Group as co-leads on data synthesis efforts. Through dedicated cross-training in theoretical biophysics and machine learning, and by hosting annual open-science hackathons, we will equip the next generation of scientists with the transdisciplinary skills required to navigate the future of molecular and cellular biology. By mapping the transition from molecular components to mesoscale emergence, this synthesis project will provide unprecedented predictive insights into cellular organization, directly advancing the foundational mission of NCEMS.

abstract_original: The unexpected appearance of new biological system properties—emergence—is a defining feature of the molecular and cellular biosciences. At the mesoscale, one of the most profound unresolved emergent phenomena is the formation of biomolecular condensates via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). These dynamic, membraneless compartments bridge the gap between individual biomolecules and functional subcellular organelles, playing critical roles in stress response, gene regulation, and disease pathogenesis. Despite a wealth of isolated molecular, structural, and phenotypic datasets, the overarching principles governing how atomic-level interactions scale to emergent mesoscale condensate properties remain largely elusive. This Working Group proposes a community-scale synthesis project to decode the spatiotemporal emergence of biomolecular condensates by integrating massive, disparate, publicly available datasets. We will synthesize structural data (AlphaFold, PDB), high-throughput interactomics (BioGRID, STRING), spatial transcriptomics and proteomics, and thousands of publicly deposited live-cell super-resolution microscopy datasets (Image Data Resource, EMPIAR). Because this undertaking vastly exceeds the computational and domain expertise of any single laboratory, it necessitates the transdisciplinary environment and resources uniquely provided by NCEMS. To solve this long-standing puzzle, our team of biophysicists, computational biologists, AI specialists, and cell biologists will employ advanced multimodal artificial intelligence and data science techniques. Specifically, we will develop novel Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to map multi-valent molecular interaction networks and integrate them with deep learning-based image analysis models capable of extracting biophysical mesoscale properties (e.g., viscoelasticity, droplet fusion rates) from archived imaging data. By synthesizing these scales, we will answer a critical, novel question: How do sequence-level variations and dynamic cellular conditions reliably encode the emergent biophysical properties of mesoscale condensates? Beyond scientific discovery, this Working Group is designed to foster a diverse, collaborative scientific community and train the future data-savvy workforce. Our team bridges varying career stages and geographical locations, integrating trainees (graduate students and postdoctoral fellows) directly into the core analytical pipeline. Trainees will benefit from dedicated mentorship, cross-disciplinary cross-training, and rigorous instruction in cloud computing, data synthesis, and machine learning. Furthermore, this project adheres strictly to Open Science principles. All aggregated datasets, curated metadata, trained AI models, and analytical pipelines will be made freely available via public repositories, utilizing reproducible workflows (e.g., Jupyter Notebooks, Docker containers) to ensure maximum utility for the broader scientific community. Ultimately, this synthesis will yield a unified framework for mesoscale emergence, transforming isolated molecular observations into a holistic understanding of subcellular organization while establishing innovative analytical paradigms for future NCEMS initiatives.

Bridging the critical gap between individual macromolecules and complex cellular organelles, these membraneless compartments orchestrate vital processes ranging from gene regulation to cellular stress response. Despite their biological ubiquity, the fundamental molecular grammar dictating how varied atomic-level interactions—particularly among intrinsically disordered proteins and RNA—scale up to govern mesoscale material properties and macroscopic cellular phenotypes remains a long-standing puzzle. Currently, structural biology, spatial proteomics, and cellular biophysics generate massive, high-fidelity datasets; however, these data remain highly siloed. Individual research laboratories lack the cross-disciplinary expertise and computational infrastructure required to unify these divergent streams into a cohesive, predictive framework of mesoscale emergence. To address this, we propose a transdisciplinary Working Group to synthesize massive, publicly available molecular and cellular datasets to decode the emergent properties of biomolecular condensates. This community-scale synthesis project will leverage AI and advanced data science to integrate atomic-resolution structural predictions (AlphaFold, Protein Data Bank), intrinsically disordered protein registries (DisProt), phase-separation databases (CD-CODE, PhaSePro), global interactomes (BioGRID, STRING), and bioimaging/Cryo-ET repositories (EMPIAR, Image Data Resource). Importantly, this project will generate no new experimental data, relying entirely on the computational synthesis and harmonization of these public resources. Our working group will pursue three primary objectives: (1) Unify and harmonize these highly heterogeneous datasets to construct the first multi-scale Condensate Graph, mathematically representing the relationships between sequence-level features and mesoscale assembly. (2) Develop and train novel geometric deep learning models to predict emergent mesoscale physical properties—such as condensate liquidity, valency, and viscoelasticity—directly from these synthesized omics and structural data. (3) Map these mesoscale phase behaviors to higher-order subcellular and phenotypic outcomes, specifically focusing on how the dysregulation of this emergent grammar correlates with known disease markers. This endeavor directly aligns with the core mission of NCEMS. The sheer scale and complexity of bridging atomistic biophysics with cellular phenomics via machine learning necessitate a collaborative, transdisciplinary approach that transcends the capabilities of any single research group. Our proposed Working Group deliberately brings together experts in artificial intelligence, computational biophysics, structural biology, and spatial multi-omics from geographically diverse institutions and varying career stages. Central to our proposal is a steadfast commitment to workforce development and Open Science. Graduate students and postdoctoral fellows will be integrated as core analysts, receiving cross-training in AI-driven omics integration, biophysical modeling, and rigorous reproducible data science practices. Furthermore, in strict adherence to community-created open science policies, all integrated databases, machine learning codebases, and analytical workflows will be released publicly under FAIR principles. Ultimately, this data synthesis will solve fundamental mysteries of mesoscale biological emergence, providing the broader scientific community with a powerful new computational lens to understand subcellular organization.

By synthesizing massive public datasets through a collaborative, community-scale effort, the PREC Working Group will illuminate the foundational rules of mesoscale emergence, transforming our understanding of cellular organization and establishing new computational paradigms for the biosciences.
